steps.title: 지루해요, 신나요
steps.goal: -ed/-ing 형용사로 기분과 일을 구분해 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 토론토 닷새째 비 오는 오후, 클로이 부모님 집 거실. 창밖에 비가 내리고, 소파에 앉은 지우가 턱을 괴고 있고, 옆에서 클로이가 웃으며 손가락 두 개로 무언가를 설명함(글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "I’m so bored." (지루해요, 신나요). Goal: -ed/-ing 형용사로 기분과 일을 구분해 말하기. Today's scene: 토론토 닷새째 비 오는 오후, 클로이 부모님 집 거실. 창밖에 비가 내리고, 소파에 앉은 지우가 턱을 괴고 있고, 옆에서 클로이가 웃으며 손가락 두 개로 무언가를 설명함. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Chloe, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I’m so bored.".

steps.when: 내가 지루함을 *느낄* 때 써요. 느끼는 쪽은 *-ed*.
steps.extra: I’m so bored. Let’s do something!
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I’m so bored." (너무 지루해요. 너무 심심해요.). When to use it: 내가 지루함을 느낄 때 써요. 느끼는 쪽은 -ed. Note: I’m so bored. Let’s do something!
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "It was really ___ing.".

steps.when: 일·물건·장소가 어땠는지 말해요. 그런 느낌을 *주는* 쪽은 *-ing*(사람도 돼요).
steps.extra: It was really boring. · It was really exciting.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "It was really ___ing." (정말 ~했어요.). When to use it: 일·물건·장소가 어땠는지 말해요. 그런 느낌을 주는 쪽은 -ing(사람도 돼요). Note: It was really boring. · It was really exciting.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I’m interested in ___.".

steps.when: 관심 있는 것을 말해요. in 뒤에는 명사나 *-ing*.
steps.extra: I’m interested in old buildings. · I’m interested in design.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I’m interested in ___." (~에 관심 있어요.). When to use it: 관심 있는 것을 말해요. in 뒤에는 명사나 -ing. Note: I’m interested in old buildings. · I’m interested in design.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("A Rainy Day · 토론토 닷새째 오후, 클로이 부모님 집 거실에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: A Rainy Day · 토론토 닷새째 오후, 클로이 부모님 집 거실에서

lines.en: Ugh, it’s still raining. You look a little down, Jiwoo.
lines.ko: 아휴, 아직도 비가 오네요. 지우 씨, 좀 처져 보여요.

lines.en: {{I’m so bored.}} I’m tired of the rain. I wanted to walk by the lake today.
lines.ko: 너무 심심해요. 비가 지겨워요. 오늘 호숫가를 걷고 싶었거든요.

lines.en: I know. So, how was the museum yesterday? Tell me the truth!
lines.ko: 그러게요. 그럼 어제 박물관은 어땠어요? 솔직하게 말해 줘요!

lines.en: Well… I was so boring there.
lines.ko: 음… 저 거기서 너무 지루‘한’ 사람이었어요.

lines.en: Oh, you mean you were bored! “Bored” is how you feel. “Boring” is what makes you feel that way.
lines.ko: 아, 지우 씨가 지루했다는 거죠! bored는 느끼는 쪽, boring은 그런 느낌을 주는 쪽이에요.

lines.en: Oh, it’s a bit confusing! Okay. The museum was boring, and I was bored.
lines.ko: 아, 좀 헷갈리네요! 알겠어요. 박물관이 지루했고, 저는 지루했어요.

lines.en: Yes! That sounded so natural! Honestly, I was bored to death, too.
lines.ko: 맞아요! 정말 자연스러웠어요! 사실 저도 지루해 죽는 줄 알았어요.

lines.en: Ha! But the crown room was great. {{It was really}} interesting.
lines.ko: 하하! 그래도 왕관 방은 좋았어요. 정말 흥미로웠어요.

lines.en: True! So, what kind of places do you like?
lines.ko: 맞아요! 그럼 어떤 곳을 좋아해요?

lines.en: {{I’m interested in}} buildings and design. Daniel says Chicago has great buildings.
lines.ko: 건물이랑 디자인에 관심 있어요. 대니얼이 시카고에 멋진 건물이 많대요.

lines.en: Ooh, Chicago! I’m so excited for you. Maybe I can come, too!
lines.ko: 오, 시카고! 제가 다 신나네요. 어쩌면 저도 갈 수 있을지도요!

lines.en: Really? That’s amazing! I’m excited about the trip already.
lines.ko: 정말요? 너무 좋다! 벌써 여행 생각에 신나요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "A Rainy Day · 토론토 닷새째 오후, 클로이 부모님 집 거실에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Chloe: "Ugh, it’s still raining. You look a little down, Jiwoo." (아휴, 아직도 비가 오네요. 지우 씨, 좀 처져 보여요.)
2. Jiwoo: "I’m so bored. I’m tired of the rain. I wanted to walk by the lake today." (너무 심심해요. 비가 지겨워요. 오늘 호숫가를 걷고 싶었거든요.)
3. Chloe: "I know. So, how was the museum yesterday? Tell me the truth!" (그러게요. 그럼 어제 박물관은 어땠어요? 솔직하게 말해 줘요!)
4. Jiwoo: "Well… I was so boring there." (음… 저 거기서 너무 지루‘한’ 사람이었어요.)
5. Chloe: "Oh, you mean you were bored! “Bored” is how you feel. “Boring” is what makes you feel that way." (아, 지우 씨가 지루했다는 거죠! bored는 느끼는 쪽, boring은 그런 느낌을 주는 쪽이에요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Oh, it’s a bit confusing! Okay. The museum was boring, and I was bored." (아, 좀 헷갈리네요! 알겠어요. 박물관이 지루했고, 저는 지루했어요.)
7. Chloe: "Yes! That sounded so natural! Honestly, I was bored to death, too." (맞아요! 정말 자연스러웠어요! 사실 저도 지루해 죽는 줄 알았어요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Ha! But the crown room was great. It was really interesting." (하하! 그래도 왕관 방은 좋았어요. 정말 흥미로웠어요.)
9. Chloe: "True! So, what kind of places do you like?" (맞아요! 그럼 어떤 곳을 좋아해요?)
10. Jiwoo: "I’m interested in buildings and design. Daniel says Chicago has great buildings." (건물이랑 디자인에 관심 있어요. 대니얼이 시카고에 멋진 건물이 많대요.)
11. Chloe: "Ooh, Chicago! I’m so excited for you. Maybe I can come, too!" (오, 시카고! 제가 다 신나네요. 어쩌면 저도 갈 수 있을지도요!)
12. Jiwoo: "Really? That’s amazing! I’m excited about the trip already." (정말요? 너무 좋다! 벌써 여행 생각에 신나요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Chloe. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: I’m so bored. / I’m interested in ___.
head: 일·물건 (-ing)
내 기분 (-ed)
이렇게 말해요
rows: The museum was boring. I was bored.
The game was really exciting. I was so excited.
The map was a bit confusing. I was confused.
The news was shocking. We were shocked.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: I’m so bored. / I’m interested in ___. / It was really ___ing. Table (일·물건 (-ing) → 내 기분 (-ed)):
- boring 지루한 → bored 지루해하는
- exciting 신나는 → excited 신난
- confusing 헷갈리게 하는 → confused 헷갈리는
- shocking 충격적인 → shocked 충격받은
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
The museum was *boring*. 박물관이 지루했어요. — 지루함을 *주는* 쪽
I was *bored*. 저는 지루했어요. — 지루함을 *느끼는* 사람
사람에게도 써요: I was boring. 나는 지루한 사람이었다
be interested in · excited about · tired of

I’m *interested in* buildings. 건물에 관심 있어요.
I’m *excited about* the trip. 여행 생각에 신나요.
I’m *tired of* the rain. 비가 지겨워요.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- -ing 주는 쪽 · -ed 느끼는 쪽: The museum was boring. 박물관이 지루했어요. — 지루함을 주는 쪽 / I was bored. 저는 지루했어요. — 지루함을 느끼는 사람 / 사람에게도 써요: I was boring. 나는 지루한 사람이었다
- be interested in · excited about · tired of: I’m interested in buildings. 건물에 관심 있어요. / I’m excited about the trip. 여행 생각에 신나요. / I’m tired of the rain. 비가 지겨워요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’m interested on podcasts. → I’m interested in podcasts. (interested 뒤에는 in.)
- I’m exciting about the trip. → I’m excited about the trip. (‘~ 생각에 신나요’는 excited about.)
- I’m tired of wait. → I’m tired of waiting. (of 뒤에 동사가 오면 -ing.)
- I was bored to dead. → I was bored to death. (‘지루해 죽겠다’는 to death(명사).)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: -ing 주는 쪽 · -ed 느끼는 쪽: The museum was boring. 박물관이 지루했어요. — 지루함을 주는 쪽I was bored. 저는 지루했어요. — 지루함을 느끼는 사람사람에게도 써요: I was boring. 나는 지루한 사람이었다

I’m exciting about the trip. → I’m excited about the trip.
I’m tired of wait. → I’m tired of waiting.
I was bored to dead. → I was bored to death.

steps.note: 예) the museum / boring → It was really boring. I was so bored. · 선생님이 How was ___? 하고 물어요.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) the museum / boring → It was really boring. I was so bored. · 선생님이 How was ___? 하고 물어요. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): the museum / boring | the game / exciting | the news / shocking | the long line / annoying.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "I’m so bored." (지루해요, 신나요); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I’m so bored." / "It was really ___ing." / "I’m interested in ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 지루하고 지겨울 때: "That movie was so boring." (그 영화 정말 지루했어요., 보통); "I was bored to death." (지루해 죽는 줄 알았어요., 친근); "I’m tired of ___." (~가 지겨워요., 보통)
- 신나고 놀랄 때: "The game was exciting." (경기가 신났어요., 보통); "I’m excited about the trip." (여행 생각에 신나요., 보통); "That’s amazing!" (정말 대단해요! 너무 좋다!, 친근)
- 헷갈릴 때 · 관심 보일 때: "It’s a bit confusing." (좀 헷갈려요., 보통); "I’m confused." ((제가) 헷갈려요., 보통); "It sounds interesting." (재미있겠네요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: -ed · -ing 짝 더 보기

*tired* 피곤한 · *tiring* 피곤하게 하는
*amazed* 놀란 · *amazing* 놀라운
*annoyed* 짜증 난 · *annoying* 짜증 나게 하는
*satisfied* 만족한 — I’m satisfied with my room.
즐길 거리 낱말

*entertainment* 오락, 즐길 거리
*stream* a show (인터넷으로) 프로그램을 보다 · *binge-watch* 몰아 보다
*pop* music 대중음악, 팝 · a new *album* 새 앨범

A: How was the museum?   B: Honestly, it was really ___. I was so ___.

낱말 상자: boring · bored · in · excited
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- -ed · -ing 짝 더 보기: tired 피곤한 · tiring 피곤하게 하는 / amazed 놀란 · amazing 놀라운 / annoyed 짜증 난 · annoying 짜증 나게 하는 / satisfied 만족한 — I’m satisfied with my room.
- 즐길 거리 낱말: entertainment 오락, 즐길 거리 / stream a show (인터넷으로) 프로그램을 보다 · binge-watch 몰아 보다 / pop music 대중음악, 팝 · a new album 새 앨범 / a cooking channel 요리 채널
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: How was the museum? B: Honestly, it was really ___. I was so ___. / A: Ha! So, what are you interested ___? B: Design! And I’m so ___ about the trip. / 낱말 상자: boring · bored · in · excited
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: confused (헷갈리는, 어리둥절한), annoyed (짜증 난), shocked (충격받은), satisfied (만족한), binge-watch ((드라마 등을) 몰아 보다), podcast (팟캐스트), video (영상, 동영상), magazine (잡지), radio (라디오), album (앨범), channel (채널), producer (제작자, 프로듀서).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: The trip was long and tiring.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: bored (지루해하는, 심심한) — "I’m so bored."; boring (지루한) — "The museum was boring."; excited (신난, 들뜬) — "I’m excited about the trip."; exciting (신나는) — "The game was exciting."; interested (관심 있는) — "I’m interested in design."; interesting (흥미로운, 재미있는) — "It sounds interesting."; confusing (헷갈리게 하는) — "It’s a bit confusing."; tiring (피곤하게 하는, 힘든) — "The trip was long and tiring."; annoying (짜증 나게 하는) — "The noise is annoying."; pop (대중음악, 팝) — "I like old pop songs."; stream ((인터넷으로) 실시간 보다·듣다) — "We streamed a show."; entertainment (오락, 즐길 거리) — "TV is my favorite entertainment.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What do you do on a boring day?
I watch videos. / I listen to podcasts.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What do you do on a boring day?" (hint on screen: I watch videos. / I listen to podcasts.)
- "What are you interested in these days?" (hint on screen: I’m interested in ___.)
- "What was really exciting for you this year?" (hint on screen: ___ was really exciting.)
- "What are you tired of these days?" (hint on screen: I’m tired of ___.)
- "Tell me about a boring movie or show. How did you feel?" (hint on screen: It was really boring. I was bored to death.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Nobody Was Bored
steps.text: It rained all day. Jiwoo spent the afternoon at Chloe’s parents’ house. Chloe’s dad turned on the radio. It was playing songs from an old pop album. Chloe’s mom had a magazine with photos of Chicago. Jiwoo found them extremely interesting. Then Chloe showed Jiwoo a short travel video. She made it herself. “You should start your own channel!” said Jiwoo. Chloe *shook her head*. “No way. But maybe I’ll be a producer one day.” *In spite of* the rain, nobody was bored. They binge-watched a funny show. After that, Jiwoo helped *clean up* the living room. Chloe’s mom smiled. “What a nice guest!”
steps.gloss: extremely 매우, 몹시 · herself (그녀가) 직접 · shake one’s head 고개를 젓다 · producer 제작자 · in spite of ~에도 불구하고 · binge-watch 몰아 보다 · clean up 치우다, 정리하다
questions: What did Chloe make herself?
What did Jiwoo do after the show?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Nobody Was Bored". Text: "It rained all day. Jiwoo spent the afternoon at Chloe’s parents’ house. Chloe’s dad turned on the radio. It was playing songs from an old pop album. Chloe’s mom had a magazine with photos of Chicago. Jiwoo found them extremely interesting. Then Chloe showed Jiwoo a short travel video. She made it herself. “You should start your own channel!” said Jiwoo. Chloe shook her head. “No way. But maybe I’ll be a producer one day.” In spite of the rain, nobody was bored. They binge-watched a funny show. After that, Jiwoo helped clean up the living room. Chloe’s mom smiled. “What a nice guest!”" Words: extremely 매우, 몹시 · herself (그녀가) 직접 · shake one’s head 고개를 젓다 · producer 제작자 · in spite of ~에도 불구하고 · binge-watch 몰아 보다 · clean up 치우다, 정리하다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Chloe make herself?" / "What did Jiwoo do after the show?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘I’m so bored.’로 지루하고 심심한 기분을 말할 수 있어요.
‘It was really ___ing.’로 일·장소가 어땠는지 말하고, -ing와 -ed를 구분할 수 있어요.
‘I’m interested in ___.’로 관심 있는 것을 말할 수 있어요.

Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘I’m so bored.’로 지루하고 심심한 기분을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘It was really ___ing.’로 일·장소가 어땠는지 말하고, -ing와 -ed를 구분할 수 있어요.
- ‘I’m interested in ___.’로 관심 있는 것을 말할 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 왜 골랐어요?
steps.goal: 고른 이유를 묻고 because로 이유를 말하고, 이해했다고 답하기
steps.scene_desc: 토론토 닷새째 저녁, 작은 호텔 방 창가. 지우가 의자에 앉아 휴대폰으로 통화하며 웃고, 탁자 위에는 기차 그림과 비행기 그림이 있는 여행 안내 책자 두 권이 펼쳐져 있음(글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Why did you choose Toronto?" (왜 골랐어요?). Goal: 고른 이유를 묻고 because로 이유를 말하고, 이해했다고 답하기. Today's scene: 토론토 닷새째 저녁, 작은 호텔 방 창가. 지우가 의자에 앉아 휴대폰으로 통화하며 웃고, 탁자 위에는 기차 그림과 비행기 그림이 있는 여행 안내 책자 두 권이 펼쳐져 있음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Daniel, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Why did you choose ___?".

steps.when: 상대가 고른 이유를 물어요. choose는 ‘고르다’, did 뒤라서 동사원형.
steps.extra: Why did you choose this hotel? · Why did you choose Toronto?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Why did you choose ___?" (왜 ~를 골랐어요?). When to use it: 상대가 고른 이유를 물어요. choose는 ‘고르다’, did 뒤라서 동사원형. Note: Why did you choose this hotel? · Why did you choose Toronto?
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I chose it because ___.".

steps.when: 고른 이유를 말해요. chose는 choose의 과거형, because 뒤에는 *이유*(주어+동사).
steps.extra: I chose it because it was cheap.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I chose it because ___." (~해서 그걸 골랐어요.). When to use it: 고른 이유를 말해요. chose는 choose의 과거형, because 뒤에는 이유(주어+동사). Note: I chose it because it was cheap.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "That makes sense.".

steps.when: 상대가 말한 이유가 이해될 때 맞장구쳐요.
steps.extra: 비슷한 말: I see. · Good choice.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "That makes sense." (그렇겠네요. 이해돼요.). When to use it: 상대가 말한 이유가 이해될 때 맞장구쳐요. Note: 비슷한 말: I see. · Good choice.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("A Call from Daniel · 토론토 호텔 방에서, 대니얼과 통화") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: A Call from Daniel · 토론토 호텔 방에서, 대니얼과 통화

lines.en: Hi, Jiwoo! Did you get my message?
lines.ko: 안녕하세요, 지우 씨! 제 메시지 받았어요?

lines.en: Yes! Toronto is great. Chloe is showing me everything.
lines.ko: 네! 토론토 정말 좋아요. 클로이가 다 보여 주고 있어요.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: Why did you choose ___? / I chose it because ___. / That makes sense. Table (고른 것 → 이유 (because)):
- Toronto 토론토 → because my friend lives there
- this hotel 이 호텔 → because it had good reviews
- this café 이 카페 → because it was close to my place
- this laptop 이 노트북 → because the price was right
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I chose it *because* it was cheap. 싸서 골랐어요.
It was cheap, *so* I chose it. 싸서, 그래서 골랐어요.
대답은 Because ~.로 시작해도 돼요.

choose → *chose* 고르다 → 골랐다
I *decided to* go. 가기로 했어요.
*That’s why* I’m at a hotel. 그래서 호텔에 있는 거예요.

I chose it because it was cheap.

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- because + 이유 · so + 결과: I chose it because it was cheap. 싸서 골랐어요. / It was cheap, so I chose it. 싸서, 그래서 골랐어요. / 대답은 Because ~.로 시작해도 돼요.
- chose · decided to · That’s why: choose → chose 고르다 → 골랐다 / I decided to go. 가기로 했어요. / That’s why I’m at a hotel. 그래서 호텔에 있는 거예요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Why did you chose Toronto? → Why did you choose Toronto? (did 뒤에는 동사원형.)
- I choosed it because it was cheap. → I chose it because it was cheap. (choose의 과거형은 chose.)
- I decided go with her. → I decided to go with her. (decided 뒤에는 to + 동사원형.)
- I chose it because of it was close. → I chose it because it was close. (주어+동사 앞에는 because(because of 뒤에는 명사).)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) the train / it was cheaper → I chose it because it was cheaper. · 선생님이 Why did you choose ___? 하고 물어요. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): Toronto / it’s Chloe’s hometown | this hotel / it had good reviews | the train / it was cheaper | this café / it was close to my place.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "Why did you choose Toronto?" (왜 골랐어요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Why did you choose ___?" / "I chose it because ___." / "That makes sense.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: It was close to my place.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 이유 말하기: "It was close to my place." (우리 집에서 가까웠어요., 보통); "The price was right." (가격이 괜찮았어요., 보통); "It had good reviews." (후기가 좋았어요., 보통); "I didn’t have much choice." (고를 게 별로 없었어요., 보통)
- 그래서 한 일: "So I decided to ___." (그래서 ~하기로 했어요., 보통); "That’s why I ___." (그래서 ~한 거예요., 보통); "To be honest, ___." (솔직히 말하면 ~., 보통)
- 듣고 맞장구치기: "I see." (그렇군요., 보통); "Good choice." (잘 골랐네요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.

낱말 상자: choose · because · sense · so
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- choose 가족 낱말: choose 고르다 → choice 선택 / decide 결정하다 → decision 결정 / select (목록에서) 고르다 — Select a seat. / an option 선택지 — We have two options.
- so · therefore · rely on: so 그래서(말) · therefore 그러므로(글, 격식) / I rely on reviews. 후기에 많이 기대요. / Price is my first consideration. 가격을 제일 먼저 따져요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Why did you ___ this hotel? B: I chose it ___ it had good reviews. / A: That makes ___. B: And it was close to the lake, ___ I booked it. / 낱말 상자: choose · because · sense · so
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: choose (고르다), select ((목록에서) 선택하다), option (선택지, 옵션), location (위치), quality (품질), excellent (아주 훌륭한), decide (결정하다), review (후기, 리뷰), price (가격), convenient (편리한), train (기차), plane (비행기).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: To be honest, I was tired.
My primary reason was the location.
It was cheaper. Therefore, she chose it.
I chose it because it was close.
It was cheap, so I bought it.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: choice (선택; 고를 수 있는 것) — "Good choice!"; decision (결정) — "It was a big decision."; honest (솔직한) — "To be honest, I was tired."; reason (이유) — "My reason was simple."; primary (주된, 가장 중요한) — "My primary reason was the location."; consideration (고려할 점) — "Price is my first consideration."; therefore (그러므로(글, 격식)) — "It was cheaper. Therefore, she chose it."; why (왜) — "Why did you choose it?"; because (~ 때문에, ~해서) — "I chose it because it was close."; so (그래서) — "It was cheap, so I bought it.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Think of a café you often go to. Why did you choose it?
What’s more important to you, price or quality?
How do you choose a restaurant? What do you rely on?
I rely on reviews. / I ask my friends.
Why did you choose to learn English?
I chose to learn English because ___.
Tell me about a small decision you made this week.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Think of a café you often go to. Why did you choose it?" (hint on screen: I chose it because ___.)
- "What’s more important to you, price or quality?" (hint on screen: Quality, because ___. / Price. So I ___.)
- "How do you choose a restaurant? What do you rely on?" (hint on screen: I rely on reviews. / I ask my friends.)
- "Why did you choose to learn English?" (hint on screen: I chose to learn English because ___.)
- "Tell me about a small decision you made this week." (hint on screen: I decided to ___ because ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: Think of a café you often go to. Why did you choose it?
What’s more important to you, price or quality?
How do you choose a restaurant? What do you rely on?
Why did you choose to learn English?
Tell me about a small decision you made this week.

steps.title: Jiwoo’s Choice
steps.text: After the call, Jiwoo looked at her options again. The train took most of the day, but it had excellent reviews and big windows. Her *primary* reason was simple: she wanted to see the country. Price was another consideration, and the train was cheaper. Therefore, Jiwoo *chose to* take the train. She didn’t want to *rely on* Chloe for everything, so she selected a window seat herself. Then she called Daniel again. “You understand the importance of a good view!” he laughed. Suddenly, the call was *cut off*. Jiwoo laughed and sent him a message.
steps.gloss: primary 주된 · consideration 고려할 점 · therefore 그러므로 · choose to ~하기로 하다 · rely on ~에 기대다 · importance 중요성 · cut off (전화가) 끊기다
questions: What was Jiwoo’s primary reason for the train?
What happened at the end of the second call?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Jiwoo’s Choice". Text: "After the call, Jiwoo looked at her options again. The train took most of the day, but it had excellent reviews and big windows. Her primary reason was simple: she wanted to see the country. Price was another consideration, and the train was cheaper. Therefore, Jiwoo chose to take the train. She didn’t want to rely on Chloe for everything, so she selected a window seat herself. Then she called Daniel again. “You understand the importance of a good view!” he laughed. Suddenly, the call was cut off. Jiwoo laughed and sent him a message." Words: primary 주된 · consideration 고려할 점 · therefore 그러므로 · choose to ~하기로 하다 · rely on ~에 기대다 · importance 중요성 · cut off (전화가) 끊기다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What was Jiwoo’s primary reason for the train?" / "What happened at the end of the second call?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘Why did you choose ___?’로 고른 이유를 물을 수 있어요.
‘I chose it because ___.’로 이유를 말하고, so로 결과를 이어 말할 수 있어요.
‘That makes sense.’로 이해했다고 맞장구칠 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘Why did you choose ___?’로 고른 이유를 물을 수 있어요.
- ‘I chose it because ___.’로 이유를 말하고, so로 결과를 이어 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘That makes sense.’로 이해했다고 맞장구칠 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

lessons.title: 그때 기분
lessons.goal: 그때 기분을 묻고 when으로 말하고, 공감하기

steps.title: 그때 기분
steps.goal: 그때 기분을 묻고 when으로 말하고, 공감하기
steps.scene_desc: 5월 초 저녁, 비가 갠 토론토 호숫가 공원 벤치. 지우가 휴대폰을 들고 화면 속 마야(서울은 아침, 커피잔을 든 모습)와 영상 통화를 하며, 한 손으로 비행기가 흔들리는 흉내를 냄(화면·주변에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "How did you feel?" (그때 기분). Goal: 그때 기분을 묻고 when으로 말하고, 공감하기. Today's scene: 5월 초 저녁, 비가 갠 토론토 호숫가 공원 벤치. 지우가 휴대폰을 들고 화면 속 마야(서울은 아침, 커피잔을 든 모습)와 영상 통화를 하며, 한 손으로 비행기가 흔들리는 흉내를 냄. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Maya, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "How did you feel?".

steps.when: 지난 일을 듣고 그때 기분을 물어요. 지나간 일이라 *did* + feel.
steps.extra: 대답: I was so nervous. · I was over the moon!
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "How did you feel?" (기분이 어땠어요?). When to use it: 지난 일을 듣고 그때 기분을 물어요. 지나간 일이라 did + feel. Note: 대답: I was so nervous. · I was over the moon!
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I was so ___ when ___.".

steps.when: 기분 낱말 뒤에 *when + 문장*을 붙여 ‘언제’ 그랬는지 말해요.
steps.extra: I was so nervous when the plane took off.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I was so ___ when ___." (~할 때 너무 ~했어요.). When to use it: 기분 낱말 뒤에 when + 문장을 붙여 ‘언제’ 그랬는지 말해요. Note: I was so nervous when the plane took off.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "That must have been ___.".

steps.when: 상대의 지난 이야기를 듣고 그때 기분을 짐작해 공감해요. 통째로 익혀요.
steps.extra: That must have been scary. · That must have been fun.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "That must have been ___." (~했겠네요.). When to use it: 상대의 지난 이야기를 듣고 그때 기분을 짐작해 공감해요. 통째로 익혀요. Note: That must have been scary. · That must have been fun.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("How Did You Feel? · 토론토의 저녁(서울은 아침), 마야와 영상 통화") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: How Did You Feel? · 토론토의 저녁(서울은 아침), 마야와 영상 통화

lines.en: Good morning from Seoul! Jiwoo, you never told me about the flight. {{How did you feel}}?
lines.ko: 서울에서 좋은 아침! 지우 씨, 비행기 얘기는 안 해 줬잖아요. 기분이 어땠어요?

lines.en: Honestly? {{I was so}} nervous {{when}} the plane took off. It was my first long flight.
lines.ko: 솔직히요? 비행기가 이륙할 때 너무 떨렸어요. 처음 타 보는 긴 비행이었거든요.

lines.en: I know how you feel. What happened?
lines.ko: 그 기분 알아요. 무슨 일 있었어요?

lines.en: The plane shook a little. It really frightened me. I almost screamed!
lines.ko: 비행기가 조금 흔들렸어요. 정말 겁났어요. 소리 지를 뻔했다니까요!

lines.en: Oh no! {{That must have been}} scary.
lines.ko: 저런! 무서웠겠어요.

lines.en: It was. But Chloe said, “Just breathe.” Then we ended up watching dramas for six hours or something.
lines.ko: 네. 그런데 클로이가 “숨 크게 쉬어요.” 했어요. 그러고는 결국 드라마를 여섯 시간인가 봤어요.

lines.en: Ha! And what was your first reaction to Toronto?
lines.ko: 하하! 그럼 토론토를 처음 봤을 때 반응은요?

lines.en: {{I was so}} excited {{when}} I saw the lake. I couldn’t stop smiling. But then I left my jacket on the plane!
lines.ko: 호수를 봤을 때 너무 신났어요. 웃음이 멈추질 않았어요. 그런데 비행기에 재킷을 두고 내렸어요!

lines.en: Oh no! Did you get it back?
lines.ko: 이런! 다시 찾았어요?

lines.en: Yes. A flight attendant ran after me with it. I felt so embarrassed, but I was relieved.
lines.ko: 네. 승무원이 재킷을 들고 뛰어왔어요. 너무 창피했지만 안심됐어요.

lines.en: What a relief! I’d feel the same way. And next stop, Chicago. You’ve got this!
lines.ko: 정말 다행이다! 저라도 그랬을 거예요. 다음은 시카고네요. 잘할 거예요!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "How Did You Feel? · 토론토의 저녁(서울은 아침), 마야와 영상 통화", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Maya: "Good morning from Seoul! Jiwoo, you never told me about the flight. How did you feel?" (서울에서 좋은 아침! 지우 씨, 비행기 얘기는 안 해 줬잖아요. 기분이 어땠어요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Honestly? I was so nervous when the plane took off. It was my first long flight." (솔직히요? 비행기가 이륙할 때 너무 떨렸어요. 처음 타 보는 긴 비행이었거든요.)
3. Maya: "I know how you feel. What happened?" (그 기분 알아요. 무슨 일 있었어요?)
4. Jiwoo: "The plane shook a little. It really frightened me. I almost screamed!" (비행기가 조금 흔들렸어요. 정말 겁났어요. 소리 지를 뻔했다니까요!)
5. Maya: "Oh no! That must have been scary." (저런! 무서웠겠어요.)
6. Jiwoo: "It was. But Chloe said, “Just breathe.” Then we ended up watching dramas for six hours or something." (네. 그런데 클로이가 “숨 크게 쉬어요.” 했어요. 그러고는 결국 드라마를 여섯 시간인가 봤어요.)
7. Maya: "Ha! And what was your first reaction to Toronto?" (하하! 그럼 토론토를 처음 봤을 때 반응은요?)
8. Jiwoo: "I was so excited when I saw the lake. I couldn’t stop smiling. But then I left my jacket on the plane!" (호수를 봤을 때 너무 신났어요. 웃음이 멈추질 않았어요. 그런데 비행기에 재킷을 두고 내렸어요!)
9. Maya: "Oh no! Did you get it back?" (이런! 다시 찾았어요?)
10. Jiwoo: "Yes. A flight attendant ran after me with it. I felt so embarrassed, but I was relieved." (네. 승무원이 재킷을 들고 뛰어왔어요. 너무 창피했지만 안심됐어요.)
11. Maya: "What a relief! I’d feel the same way. And next stop, Chicago. You’ve got this!" (정말 다행이다! 저라도 그랬을 거예요. 다음은 시카고네요. 잘할 거예요!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

5. Maya (you): "Oh no! That must have been scary." (저런! 무서웠겠어요.)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "It was. But Chloe said, “Just breathe.” Then we ended up watching dramas for six hours or something." (네. 그런데 클로이가 “숨 크게 쉬어요.” 했어요. 그러고는 결국 드라마를 여섯 시간인가 봤어요.)
7. Maya (you): "Ha! And what was your first reaction to Toronto?" (하하! 그럼 토론토를 처음 봤을 때 반응은요?)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "I was so excited when I saw the lake. I couldn’t stop smiling. But then I left my jacket on the plane!" (호수를 봤을 때 너무 신났어요. 웃음이 멈추질 않았어요. 그런데 비행기에 재킷을 두고 내렸어요!)
9. Maya (you): "Oh no! Did you get it back?" (이런! 다시 찾았어요?)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "Yes. A flight attendant ran after me with it. I felt so embarrassed, but I was relieved." (네. 승무원이 재킷을 들고 뛰어왔어요. 너무 창피했지만 안심됐어요.)
11. Maya (you): "What a relief! I’d feel the same way. And next stop, Chicago. You’ve got this!" (정말 다행이다! 저라도 그랬을 거예요. 다음은 시카고네요. 잘할 거예요!)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Maya. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: Jiwoo was nervous when the plane took off.
Jiwoo slept for six hours on the plane.
A flight attendant brought Jiwoo’s jacket back.
steps.teach:
True/false check. The statements on the learner's screen, each with its answer and the scene line that shows it. The answers are for you only: never say an answer or a line number before the learner has answered:
1. Jiwoo was nervous when the plane took off. → True (line 2)
2. Jiwoo slept for six hours on the plane. → False (line 6)
3. A flight attendant brought Jiwoo’s jacket back. → True (line 10)
The scene they are about:
1. Maya: "Good morning from Seoul! Jiwoo, you never told me about the flight. How did you feel?" (서울에서 좋은 아침! 지우 씨, 비행기 얘기는 안 해 줬잖아요. 기분이 어땠어요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Honestly? I was so nervous when the plane took off. It was my first long flight." (솔직히요? 비행기가 이륙할 때 너무 떨렸어요. 처음 타 보는 긴 비행이었거든요.)

6. Jiwoo: "It was. But Chloe said, “Just breathe.” Then we ended up watching dramas for six hours or something." (네. 그런데 클로이가 “숨 크게 쉬어요.” 했어요. 그러고는 결국 드라마를 여섯 시간인가 봤어요.)
7. Maya: "Ha! And what was your first reaction to Toronto?" (하하! 그럼 토론토를 처음 봤을 때 반응은요?)
8. Jiwoo: "I was so excited when I saw the lake. I couldn’t stop smiling. But then I left my jacket on the plane!" (호수를 봤을 때 너무 신났어요. 웃음이 멈추질 않았어요. 그런데 비행기에 재킷을 두고 내렸어요!)
9. Maya: "Oh no! Did you get it back?" (이런! 다시 찾았어요?)
10. Jiwoo: "Yes. A flight attendant ran after me with it. I felt so embarrassed, but I was relieved." (네. 승무원이 재킷을 들고 뛰어왔어요. 너무 창피했지만 안심됐어요.)
11. Maya: "What a relief! I’d feel the same way. And next stop, Chicago. You’ve got this!" (정말 다행이다! 저라도 그랬을 거예요. 다음은 시카고네요. 잘할 거예요!)
Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: How did you feel? / What was your first reaction?
I was so ___ when ___. / That must have been ___.
head: 기분 (I was so …)
언제 (when …)
공감하기
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: How did you feel? / What was your first reaction? / I was so ___ when ___. / That must have been ___. Table (기분 (I was so …) → 언제 (when …)):
- nervous 떨리는 → when it took off
- embarrassed 창피한 → when I left my jacket
- relieved 안심한 → when I found my bag
- disappointed 실망한 → when the show was canceled
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
when 뒤에는 *주어+동사*: I was so nervous *when* the plane took off.
앞으로 보내면 쉼표(,): *When* I saw the lake, I was so excited.

지난 일을 듣고 그때 기분을 짐작해요.
That must have been *scary*. 무서웠겠어요.
That(그 일)이 주어라서 -ing 쪽: embarrassing
errors: I was nervous when we take off.
I was nervous when we took off.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- when + 문장 — ~할 때: when 뒤에는 주어+동사: I was so nervous when the plane took off. / 앞으로 보내면 쉼표(,): When I saw the lake, I was so excited.
- That must have been ~ — ~했겠어요: 지난 일을 듣고 그때 기분을 짐작해요. / That must have been scary. 무서웠겠어요. / That(그 일)이 주어라서 -ing 쪽: embarrassing
Common mistakes on screen:
- How did you felt? → How did you feel? (did 뒤에는 동사원형 feel.)
- I was nervous when we take off. → I was nervous when we took off. (지난 일이라 when 뒤도 과거형.)
- That must have been embarrassed. → That must have been embarrassing. (그 일(That)은 -ing 쪽.)
- I was relief. → I was relieved. (relief는 명사(안도). 기분은 relieved.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: when + 문장 — ~할 때: when 뒤에는 주어+동사: I was so nervous when the plane took off.앞으로 보내면 쉼표(,): When I saw the lake, I was so excited.
That must have been ~ — ~했겠어요: 지난 일을 듣고 그때 기분을 짐작해요.That must have been scary. 무서웠겠어요.That(그 일)이 주어라서 -ing 쪽: embarrassing
mistakes: How did you felt? → How did you feel?
I was nervous when we take off. → I was nervous when we took off.
That must have been embarrassed. → That must have been embarrassing.
I was relief. → I was relieved.

steps.note: 예) nervous / the plane took off → I was so nervous when the plane took off.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) nervous / the plane took off → I was so nervous when the plane took off. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): nervous / the plane took off | excited / I saw the lake | embarrassed / I left my jacket | relieved / I found my bag.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "How did you feel?" (그때 기분); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "How did you feel?" / "I was so ___ when ___." / "That must have been ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 그때 기분 말하기: "I was really nervous." (정말 떨렸어요., 보통); "I felt so embarrassed." (너무 창피했어요., 보통); "I was a bit disappointed." (조금 실망했어요., 보통); "I was relieved when ___." (~했을 때 안심됐어요., 보통)
- 정말 기뻤을 때: "I couldn’t stop smiling." (웃음이 멈추질 않았어요., 보통); "I was over the moon." (날아갈 듯 기뻤어요., 친근)
- 공감하고 달래기: "I know how you feel." (그 기분 알아요., 보통); "I’d feel the same way." (저라도 그랬을 거예요., 보통); "What a relief!" (정말 다행이다!, 친근); "Just breathe." (숨 크게 쉬어요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: angry · mad · upset

*angry* 화난 · *mad* 화난(미국에서 친구끼리 자주 써요)
*upset* 속상한, 마음이 상한
I wasn’t mad at anyone. 누구한테도 화나지 않았어요.
I was mad at myself. 나 자신한테 화났어요.
breath 와 breathe

*breath*[브레쓰] 숨(명사) — Take a deep breath. 숨을 깊이 쉬어요.
*breathe*[브리드] 숨 쉬다(동사) — Just breathe.
*tears* of joy 기뻐서 흘리는 눈물 · *scream* 소리 지르다
steps.blank:
A: How did you ___?   B: I was so nervous ___ the plane took off.
A: That must have ___ scary.   B: It was! But I was ___ when we landed.
낱말 상자: feel · when · been · relieved
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- angry · mad · upset: angry 화난 · mad 화난(미국에서 친구끼리 자주 써요) / upset 속상한, 마음이 상한 / I wasn’t mad at anyone. 누구한테도 화나지 않았어요. / I was mad at myself. 나 자신한테 화났어요.
- breath 와 breathe: breath[브레쓰] 숨(명사) — Take a deep breath. 숨을 깊이 쉬어요. / breathe[브리드] 숨 쉬다(동사) — Just breathe. / tears of joy 기뻐서 흘리는 눈물 · scream 소리 지르다
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: How did you ___? B: I was so nervous ___ the plane took off. / A: That must have ___ scary. B: It was! But I was ___ when we landed. / 낱말 상자: feel · when · been · relieved
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: nervous (긴장한, 떨리는), embarrassed (창피한, 당황한), relieved (안심한), disappointed (실망한), scared (무서워하는, 겁먹은), upset (속상한), angry (화난), lonely (외로운), tear (눈물), laughter (웃음(소리)), smile (미소; 웃다), scream (소리 지르다; 비명).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: It was a day full of emotions.
I’m in a great mood today.
I was surprised when I saw her.
I was so excited when I saw the lake.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: emotion (감정) — "It was a day full of emotions."; mood (기분) — "I’m in a great mood today."; breath (숨, 호흡) — "Take a deep breath."; pleasure (기쁨, 즐거움) — "It was a real pleasure."; spirit (기분, 기운(주로 spirits)) — "My spirits went up."; proud (자랑스러운) — "I’m so proud of you!"; surprised (놀란) — "I was surprised when I saw her."; excited (신난, 들뜬) — "I was so excited when I saw the lake."; reaction (반응) — "What was your first reaction?"; mad (화난(친근한 말)) — "I was mad at myself.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: How did you feel at your first English class?
I was so ___ when ___. / I was really nervous.
When were you over the moon?
I was over the moon when ___.
Have you ever felt embarrassed on a trip?
Yes! I felt so embarrassed when ___. / Not really.
Your friend lost her phone on a trip. What do you say?
That must have been ___. / I know how you feel.
Ask me how I felt about something.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "How did you feel at your first English class?" (hint on screen: I was so ___ when ___. / I was really nervous.)
- "When were you over the moon?" (hint on screen: I was over the moon when ___.)
- "Have you ever felt embarrassed on a trip?" (hint on screen: Yes! I felt so embarrassed when ___. / Not really.)
- "Your friend lost her phone on a trip. What do you say?" (hint on screen: That must have been ___. / I know how you feel.)
- "Ask me how I felt about something." (hint on screen: How did you feel when ___?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

When were you over the moon?

steps.title: A Day Full of Emotions
steps.text: My first day in Toronto was full of emotions. My initial feeling was pure excitement. Then the line at passport control was so long, and I got a little upset. But when Chloe’s dad *pulled up* in his car, my mood changed immediately. At dinner, there was so much laughter. Later, alone in my hotel room, I suddenly felt lonely. There were even tears in my eyes! I wasn’t mad. I was just tired. I *ended up* looking at old photos *or something*. Then Maya sent me a message: “So proud of you!” My spirits went right up. (The room was cold that night, but that’s another story!)
steps.gloss: initial 처음의 · excitement 신남 · passport control 입국 심사 · pull up (차가) 와서 서다 · immediately 곧바로 · end up 결국 ~하게 되다 · or something ~인가 뭔가
questions: What was Jiwoo’s initial feeling?
What did Maya’s message say?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "A Day Full of Emotions". Text: "My first day in Toronto was full of emotions. My initial feeling was pure excitement. Then the line at passport control was so long, and I got a little upset. But when Chloe’s dad pulled up in his car, my mood changed immediately. At dinner, there was so much laughter. Later, alone in my hotel room, I suddenly felt lonely. There were even tears in my eyes! I wasn’t mad. I was just tired. I ended up looking at old photos or something. Then Maya sent me a message: “So proud of you!” My spirits went right up. (The room was cold that night, but that’s another story!)" Words: initial 처음의 · excitement 신남 · passport control 입국 심사 · pull up (차가) 와서 서다 · immediately 곧바로 · end up 결국 ~하게 되다 · or something ~인가 뭔가.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What was Jiwoo’s initial feeling?" / "What did Maya’s message say?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘How did you feel?’로 지난 일의 그때 기분을 물을 수 있어요.
‘I was so ___ when ___.’으로 언제 어떤 기분이었는지 말할 수 있어요.
‘That must have been ___.’ · ‘I know how you feel.’로 공감할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘How did you feel?’로 지난 일의 그때 기분을 물을 수 있어요.
- ‘I was so ___ when ___.’으로 언제 어떤 기분이었는지 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘That must have been ___.’ · ‘I know how you feel.’로 공감할 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.scene_desc: 5월 초 아침, 토론토 작은 호텔 로비의 아침 식사 자리. 지우가 커피와 머핀을 앞에 두고 노트북 화면 속 그레이스(서울은 밤, 카디건 차림, 뒤 창가에 화분)와 영상 통화하며 손을 흔듦(화면·벽에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.

frame: What have you been up to? / How long have you been ___ing?
I’ve been ___ing lately. / For two months. · Since March.
head: 요즘 하는 일 (I’ve been …)
