steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: What have you been up to? / How long have you been ___ing? / I’ve been ___ing lately. / For two months. · Since March. Table (요즘 하는 일 (I’ve been …) → 얼마나 (for · since)):
- learning English 영어 배우기 → for a year
- volunteering 자원봉사 → since March
- doing yoga 요가 → for two months
- working on a project 프로젝트 → since Monday
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
전에 시작해서 지금도 계속하는 일을 말해요.
*I’ve been* walk*ing* a lot. (I’ve = I have)
she·he는 has been: She’s been volunteering.

*for* two months 두 달 동안 — 얼마나 오래
*since* March 3월부터 — 언제 시작했나
since·for는 Lesson 11에서 더 연습해요.
errors: What have you been up to?
be up to가 한 덩어리라서 to를 빼지 않아요.
I’ve been walk a lot lately.
I’ve been walking a lot lately.
I’ve been learning English since a year.
I’ve been learning English for a year.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- have been + -ing — 요즘 계속 ~하고 있어요: 전에 시작해서 지금도 계속하는 일을 말해요. / I’ve been walking a lot. (I’ve = I have) / she·he는 has been: She’s been volunteering.
- How long ~? 대답은 for · since: for two months 두 달 동안 — 얼마나 오래 / since March 3월부터 — 언제 시작했나 / since·for는 Lesson 11에서 더 연습해요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- What have you been up? → What have you been up to? (be up to가 한 덩어리라서 to를 빼지 않아요.)
- I’ve been walk a lot lately. → I’ve been walking a lot lately. (been 뒤에는 -ing.)
- I’ve been learning English since a year. → I’ve been learning English for a year. (‘1년 동안’처럼 기간은 for.)
- It’s been age! → It’s been ages! (‘아주 오랫동안’은 항상 ages.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: have been + -ing — 요즘 계속 ~하고 있어요: 전에 시작해서 지금도 계속하는 일을 말해요.I’ve been walking a lot. (I’ve = I have)she·he는 has been: She’s been volunteering.
How long ~? 대답은 for · since: for two months 두 달 동안 — 얼마나 오래since March 3월부터 — 언제 시작했나since·for는 Lesson 11에서 더 연습해요.
mistakes: What have you been up? → What have you been up to?
I’ve been walk a lot lately. → I’ve been walking a lot lately.
I’ve been learning English since a year. → I’ve been learning English for a year.
It’s been age! → It’s been ages!

steps.note: 예) learning English / a year → I’ve been learning English for a year. · March처럼 시작한 때는 since.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) learning English / a year → I’ve been learning English for a year. · March처럼 시작한 때는 since. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): learning English / a year | volunteering / March | walking a lot / two weeks | working on a project / Monday.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: What have you been up to?
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "What have you been up to?" (요즘 어떻게 지내요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What have you been up to?" / "I’ve been ___ing lately." / "How long have you been ___ing?". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I’ve been really busy with work.
I’ve been learning ___ for a year.
I’ve been meaning to call you.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 오랜만에 만났을 때: "Long time no see." (오랜만이에요., 친근); "It’s been ages!" (정말 오래됐네요!, 친근); "How’s everything going?" (다 잘돼 가요?, 보통)
- 요즘 이야기하기: "Not much, same old." (별일 없어요, 늘 그렇죠., 친근); "I’ve been really busy with work." (요즘 일 때문에 정말 바빴어요., 보통); "Things have been crazy." (요즘 정신없었어요., 친근); "I’ve been learning ___ for a year." (~를 1년째 배우고 있어요., 보통); "I’ve been meaning to call you." (계속 전화하려고 했어요., 친근)
- 응원하고 약속하기: "Keep it up!" (계속 그렇게 해요!, 친근); "Let’s catch up soon." (조만간 밀린 얘기 해요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

steps.title: Grace’s Saturdays
steps.text: Grace has been busy lately. On Saturdays, she volunteers at an animal shelter, and she has been going there since March. She spends the entire morning with the dogs and plays catch with them. Currently, the shelter has a big project: finding homes for twelve dogs. So Grace posts a daily update online. Her favorite is Bori, a shy little dog. He has been waiting for a family for a year. Last week, a kind family met him, and Grace felt happy and sad *at the same time*. “*Once again*, I have so many stories,” she thinks. “I can’t wait to *catch up* with Jiwoo!”
steps.gloss: entire 온, 전체의 · daily update 날마다 올리는 새 소식 · shy 수줍은 · at the same time 동시에 · once again 다시 한번 · catch up 밀린 얘기를 나누다

steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "I’d like to book a table for three." (전화로 예약하기). Goal: 전화로 자리를 예약하고, 다른 시간을 묻고, 예약 이름을 말하기. Today's scene: 5월 초 아침, 토론토 호텔 방 창가 책상. 지우가 휴대폰을 귀에 대고 통화하며 메모지에 시각을 적음. 창밖은 맑은 아침 거리. 화면·종이에 글자 없이. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Ben, Jiwoo, Staff. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I’d like to book a table for ___.".

steps.en: I’d like to book a table for ___.
steps.when: 식당에 전화해서 예약할 때 첫마디로 써요. I’d like to는 want to보다 공손한 말. for 뒤에 *사람 수*.
steps.extra: I’d like to book a table for three on Saturday.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I’d like to book a table for ___." (~명 자리를 예약하고 싶어요.). When to use it: 식당에 전화해서 예약할 때 첫마디로 써요. I’d like to는 want to보다 공손한 말. for 뒤에 사람 수. Note: I’d like to book a table for three on Saturday.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Do you have anything at ___?".

steps.title: A Table for Three · 토론토의 아침, 벤과 통화한 뒤 시카고 식당에 전화

lines.en: Jiwoo, I know a great little restaurant by the river in Chicago. Why don’t you book a table?
lines.ko: 지우 씨, 시카고 강가에 아주 좋은 작은 식당을 알아요. 자리를 예약해 보면 어때요?

lines.en: Good idea! I’d like to take Chloe and Daniel there. But what do I say?
lines.ko: 좋은 생각이에요! 클로이랑 대니얼을 데려가고 싶어요. 그런데 뭐라고 말해요?

lines.en: Here’s how people really say it: “Hi, {{I’d like to book a table for}} three.”
lines.ko: 사람들은 실제로 이렇게 말해요. “안녕하세요, 세 명 자리 예약하고 싶어요.”

lines.en: Good morning, thanks for calling. How can I help you?
lines.ko: 안녕하세요, 전화 주셔서 감사합니다. 무엇을 도와드릴까요?

lines.en: Hi. I’d like to make a reservation for Saturday evening.

lines.en: Sure. For how many people?

lines.en: Three. {{Do you have anything at}} seven?
lines.ko: 세 명이요. 7시에 자리 있어요?

lines.ko: 죄송해요, 7시는 예약이 꽉 찼어요. 8시 30분은 어떠세요?

lines.en: That’s fine. Is there a deposit?

lines.en: No, only for parties of six or more. Alright, can I get a name?
lines.ko: 아니요, 여섯 분 이상 일행만요. 자, 성함이 어떻게 되세요?

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "A Table for Three · 토론토의 아침, 벤과 통화한 뒤 시카고 식당에 전화", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:

frame: I’d like to book a table for ___. / Do you have anything at ___?

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: I’d like to book a table for ___. / Do you have anything at ___? / Could you put it under ___? Table (몇 명 (for …) → 언제 (on … at …)):
- for two 두 명 → on Friday at seven
- for three 세 명 → on Saturday at eight
- for four 네 명 → tomorrow at six thirty
- for six 여섯 명 → on Sunday at noon
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I’d like to = I would like to, want to보다 공손한 말이에요.
I’d like *to book* a table. 예약하고 싶어요. · I’d like *to cancel* my reservation. 예약을 취소하고 싶어요.
뒤에 명사만 오면 to 없이: I’d like *a table* by the window.

*for* + 사람 수 → *on* + 요일 → *at* + 시각
a table *for* three *on* Saturday *at* eight thirty
이름은 *under*: Could you put it *under* Jiwoo Kim?
errors: I’d like to book a table.
I’d like 뒤에 동사가 오면 to를 넣어요.
I’d like to book a table at Saturday.
I’d like to book a table on Saturday.
A table for three person, please.
A table for three people, please.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- I’d like to + 동사원형: I’d like to = I would like to, want to보다 공손한 말이에요. / I’d like to book a table. 예약하고 싶어요. · I’d like to cancel my reservation. 예약을 취소하고 싶어요. / 뒤에 명사만 오면 to 없이: I’d like a table by the window.
- 예약할 때 말하는 순서: for + 사람 수 → on + 요일 → at + 시각 / a table for three on Saturday at eight thirty / 이름은 under: Could you put it under Jiwoo Kim?
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’d like book a table. → I’d like to book a table. (I’d like 뒤에 동사가 오면 to를 넣어요.)
- I’d like to book a table at Saturday. → I’d like to book a table on Saturday. (요일 앞에는 on.)
- We’re full booked at seven. → We’re fully booked at seven. (‘꽉 찬’은 fully booked.)
- A table for three person, please. → A table for three people, please. (둘 이상이면 people.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

I’d like to book a table at Saturday. → I’d like to book a table on Saturday.
We’re full booked at seven. → We’re fully booked at seven.
A table for three person, please. → A table for three people, please.

steps.note: 예) two / Friday · seven → I’d like to book a table for two on Friday. Do you have anything at seven?
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) two / Friday · seven → I’d like to book a table for two on Friday. Do you have anything at seven? The items (the words the learner gets for each one): two / Friday · seven | four / Sunday · noon | three / Saturday · eight thirty | six / tomorrow · six.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: I’d like to book a table for ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "I’d like to book a table for three." (전화로 예약하기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I’d like to book a table for ___." / "Do you have anything at ___?" / "Could you put it under ___?". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: We look forward to seeing you.
Can I make a change to my booking?
I’d like to cancel my reservation.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 직원이 하는 말: "For how many people?" (몇 분이세요?, 정중); "We’re fully booked at seven." (7시는 예약이 꽉 찼어요., 정중); "Could I have your number?" (전화번호를 알려 주시겠어요?, 정중); "Any additional requests?" (더 필요하신 것 있으세요?, 정중); "We look forward to seeing you." (뵙기를 기다리겠습니다., 정중)
- 손님이 하는 말: "How about eight thirty?" (8시 30분은 어때요?, 보통); "That’s fine." (좋아요, 괜찮아요., 보통); "Is there a deposit?" (예약금이 있어요?, 보통)
- 바꾸기·취소하기: "Can I make a change to my booking?" (예약을 바꿀 수 있을까요?, 보통); "I’d like to cancel my reservation." (예약을 취소하고 싶어요., 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: telephone (전화(기)), table (식탁, 테이블), terrace (테라스), reservation (예약), reserve (예약하다, 따로 잡아 두다), cancel (취소하다), party ((식당 손님) 일행), deposit (예약금, 보증금), waiting list (대기자 명단), confirmation (확인(메시지)), accommodation (숙소), facility (시설(수영장·체육관 등)).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:

steps.title: A Table by the River
steps.text: Ben’s favorite restaurant in Chicago is a small family place by the river. Not *too many* tourists know about it, so it’s always quiet. The owner cooks, and her son works there *full time*. Every May, they *put out* tables on the terrace. This morning, Jiwoo booked a table for three by telephone: Saturday at eight thirty. There’s no additional charge for the terrace. *As for* a deposit, she didn’t need one. An hour later, a confirmation text arrived: “Please reply YES to confirm.” Jiwoo replied right away. It was her first booking in English! She can’t wait to tell Ben.
steps.gloss: owner 주인 · too many 너무 많은 · full time 정규 시간으로, 전일제로 · put out (밖에) 내놓다 · additional 추가의 · charge 요금 · as for ~에 관해서는 · reply 답장하다
questions: What does the owner’s son do?
What time is the reservation?

steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Don’t forget to take your passport!" (짐 싸기). Goal: 챙길 것을 확인하고 잊지 말라고 하기. Today's scene: 5월 초 저녁, 토론토 호텔 방. 침대 위에 활짝 열린 여행 가방과 옷가지가 쌓여 있고, 지우가 노트북 화면 속 그레이스(서울의 밝은 아침 부엌)와 영상 통화하며 휴대폰 충전기를 들어 보임. 화면·소품에 글자 없이. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Grace, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Don’t forget to ___.".

steps.when: 상대에게 꼭 챙길 일을 다정하게 일러 줘요. to 뒤에 *동사원형*.

steps.teach:

Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Have you packed ___ yet?".

steps.title: Packing Night · 토론토의 저녁(서울은 아침), 그레이스와 영상 통화

lines.en: Good morning from Seoul! So, Chloe is coming to Chicago with you?
lines.ko: 서울에서 아침 인사해요! 그래서, 클로이도 시카고에 같이 가요?

lines.en: Yes! We set out tomorrow. But I always pack too much. My suitcase won’t close!
lines.ko: 네! 내일 출발해요. 그런데 저는 늘 짐을 너무 많이 싸요. 가방이 안 닫혀요!

lines.en: Let’s do it step by step. {{Have you packed}} your passport {{yet}}?
lines.ko: 하나씩 해 봐요. 여권은 챙겼어요?

lines.en: Not yet. It’s in the safe in my room.
lines.ko: 아직요. 방 금고에 있어요.

lines.en: {{Don’t forget to}} take it out before you leave!
lines.ko: 떠나기 전에 꺼내는 거 잊지 마요!

lines.en: I won’t. Oh, my phone is almost dead. {{I’d better}} charge it tonight.
lines.ko: 안 잊을게요. 아, 휴대폰 배터리가 거의 없네요. 오늘 밤에 충전해 두는 게 좋겠어요.

lines.en: Good idea. Did you exchange money? Chicago uses US dollars.
lines.ko: 좋은 생각이에요. 환전은 했어요? 시카고는 미국 달러를 써요.

lines.en: Yes, I did that today. Should I buy a new adapter for the US?
lines.ko: 네, 오늘 했어요. 미국용 어댑터를 새로 사야 할까요?

lines.en: You won’t need it. Your adapter for Canada should work in the US, too. Check the label on your charger to be sure.
lines.ko: 필요 없을 거예요. 캐나다용 어댑터가 미국에서도 될 거예요. 확실하게 하려면 충전기 표시를 확인해 봐요.

lines.en: Great. But Chloe has two cameras and a big bag of equipment!
lines.ko: 잘됐다. 그런데 클로이는 카메라 두 대에 장비 가방까지 커다란 게 있어요!

lines.en: Ha! In other words, she packs too much, too. Have a safe trip, and don’t forget to send pictures!
lines.ko: 하하! 다시 말해, 클로이도 짐을 너무 많이 싸는군요. 조심히 다녀오고, 사진 보내는 거 잊지 마요!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Packing Night · 토론토의 저녁(서울은 아침), 그레이스와 영상 통화", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Grace: "Good morning from Seoul! So, Chloe is coming to Chicago with you?" (서울에서 아침 인사해요! 그래서, 클로이도 시카고에 같이 가요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Yes! We set out tomorrow. But I always pack too much. My suitcase won’t close!" (네! 내일 출발해요. 그런데 저는 늘 짐을 너무 많이 싸요. 가방이 안 닫혀요!)
3. Grace: "Let’s do it step by step. Have you packed your passport yet?" (하나씩 해 봐요. 여권은 챙겼어요?)
4. Jiwoo: "Not yet. It’s in the safe in my room." (아직요. 방 금고에 있어요.)
5. Grace: "Don’t forget to take it out before you leave!" (떠나기 전에 꺼내는 거 잊지 마요!)
6. Jiwoo: "I won’t. Oh, my phone is almost dead. I’d better charge it tonight." (안 잊을게요. 아, 휴대폰 배터리가 거의 없네요. 오늘 밤에 충전해 두는 게 좋겠어요.)
7. Grace: "Good idea. Did you exchange money? Chicago uses US dollars." (좋은 생각이에요. 환전은 했어요? 시카고는 미국 달러를 써요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Yes, I did that today. Should I buy a new adapter for the US?" (네, 오늘 했어요. 미국용 어댑터를 새로 사야 할까요?)
9. Grace: "You won’t need it. Your adapter for Canada should work in the US, too. Check the label on your charger to be sure." (필요 없을 거예요. 캐나다용 어댑터가 미국에서도 될 거예요. 확실하게 하려면 충전기 표시를 확인해 봐요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Great. But Chloe has two cameras and a big bag of equipment!" (잘됐다. 그런데 클로이는 카메라 두 대에 장비 가방까지 커다란 게 있어요!)
11. Grace: "Ha! In other words, she packs too much, too. Have a safe trip, and don’t forget to send pictures!" (하하! 다시 말해, 클로이도 짐을 너무 많이 싸는군요. 조심히 다녀오고, 사진 보내는 거 잊지 마요!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

11. Grace (you): "Ha! In other words, she packs too much, too. Have a safe trip, and don’t forget to send pictures!" (하하! 다시 말해, 클로이도 짐을 너무 많이 싸는군요. 조심히 다녀오고, 사진 보내는 거 잊지 마요!)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Grace. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: Chloe is going to Chicago with Jiwoo.
Jiwoo’s passport is in her suitcase.
Jiwoo needs a new adapter for the US.
steps.teach:
True/false check. The statements on the learner's screen, each with its answer and the scene line that shows it. The answers are for you only: never say an answer or a line number before the learner has answered:
1. Chloe is going to Chicago with Jiwoo. → True (line 1, 2)
2. Jiwoo’s passport is in her suitcase. → False (line 4)
3. Jiwoo needs a new adapter for the US. → False (line 8, 9)
The scene they are about:
1. Grace: "Good morning from Seoul! So, Chloe is coming to Chicago with you?" (서울에서 아침 인사해요! 그래서, 클로이도 시카고에 같이 가요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Yes! We set out tomorrow. But I always pack too much. My suitcase won’t close!" (네! 내일 출발해요. 그런데 저는 늘 짐을 너무 많이 싸요. 가방이 안 닫혀요!)
3. Grace: "Let’s do it step by step. Have you packed your passport yet?" (하나씩 해 봐요. 여권은 챙겼어요?)
4. Jiwoo: "Not yet. It’s in the safe in my room." (아직요. 방 금고에 있어요.)
5. Grace: "Don’t forget to take it out before you leave!" (떠나기 전에 꺼내는 거 잊지 마요!)
6. Jiwoo: "I won’t. Oh, my phone is almost dead. I’d better charge it tonight." (안 잊을게요. 아, 휴대폰 배터리가 거의 없네요. 오늘 밤에 충전해 두는 게 좋겠어요.)
7. Grace: "Good idea. Did you exchange money? Chicago uses US dollars." (좋은 생각이에요. 환전은 했어요? 시카고는 미국 달러를 써요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Yes, I did that today. Should I buy a new adapter for the US?" (네, 오늘 했어요. 미국용 어댑터를 새로 사야 할까요?)
9. Grace: "You won’t need it. Your adapter for Canada should work in the US, too. Check the label on your charger to be sure." (필요 없을 거예요. 캐나다용 어댑터가 미국에서도 될 거예요. 확실하게 하려면 충전기 표시를 확인해 봐요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Great. But Chloe has two cameras and a big bag of equipment!" (잘됐다. 그런데 클로이는 카메라 두 대에 장비 가방까지 커다란 게 있어요!)
11. Grace: "Ha! In other words, she packs too much, too. Have a safe trip, and don’t forget to send pictures!" (하하! 다시 말해, 클로이도 짐을 너무 많이 싸는군요. 조심히 다녀오고, 사진 보내는 거 잊지 마요!)
Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: Have you packed ___ yet? / Is everything ready?
head: 확인 (Have you packed … yet?)
대답
일러 주기 (Don’t forget to …)
rows: Don’t forget to charge your phone.
Don’t forget to put it on.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: Have you packed ___ yet? / Is everything ready? / Don’t forget to ___. / I’d better ___. Table (확인 (Have you packed … yet?) → 대답):
- your passport 여권 → Not yet.
- your charger 충전기 → Yes, I have.
- your toothbrush 칫솔 → Oops, not yet!
- sunscreen 선크림 → Yes, it’s in my bag.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I’d better = I had better: 안 하면 곤란하니까 ~하는 게 좋겠다.
I’d better *charge* my phone. 뒤에 to 없이 동사원형.
부정: I’d better *not* forget.
Don’t forget to ~ · Have you ~ yet?

Don’t forget *to* take your passport. 여권 챙기는 거 잊지 마요.
대답: I won’t. 안 잊을게요. · Thanks!
*Have* you *packed* your charger *yet*? — Yes, I have. · Not yet.
errors: I’d better not to forget it.
Have you pack your passport yet?
Have you packed your passport yet?
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- I’d better + 동사원형: I’d better = I had better: 안 하면 곤란하니까 ~하는 게 좋겠다. / I’d better charge my phone. 뒤에 to 없이 동사원형. / 부정: I’d better not forget.
- Don’t forget to ~ · Have you ~ yet?: Don’t forget to take your passport. 여권 챙기는 거 잊지 마요. / 대답: I won’t. 안 잊을게요. · Thanks! / Have you packed your charger yet? — Yes, I have. · Not yet.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’d better to charge it. → I’d better charge it. (had better 뒤에는 to 없이.)
- I’d better not to forget it. → I’d better not forget it. (had better not 뒤에도 동사원형.)
- Don’t forget bring it. → Don’t forget to bring it. (forget 뒤에 to + 동사원형.)
- Have you pack your passport yet? → Have you packed your passport yet? (have 뒤에는 packed.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: I’d better + 동사원형: I’d better = I had better: 안 하면 곤란하니까 ~하는 게 좋겠다.I’d better charge my phone. 뒤에 to 없이 동사원형.부정: I’d better not forget.
Don’t forget to ~ · Have you ~ yet?: Don’t forget to take your passport. 여권 챙기는 거 잊지 마요.대답: I won’t. 안 잊을게요. · Thanks!Have you packed your charger yet? — Yes, I have. · Not yet.
mistakes: I’d better to charge it. → I’d better charge it.
I’d better not to forget it. → I’d better not forget it.
Don’t forget bring it. → Don’t forget to bring it.
Have you pack your passport yet? → Have you packed your passport yet?

steps.note: 예) your passport / take it → Have you packed your passport yet? Don’t forget to take it!
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) your passport / take it → Have you packed your passport yet? Don’t forget to take it! The items (the words the learner gets for each one): your passport / take it | your charger / charge your phone | your toothbrush / pack it | sunscreen / put it on.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "Don’t forget to take your passport!" (짐 싸기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Don’t forget to ___." / "Have you packed ___ yet?" / "I’d better ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: 저는 늘 짐을 너무 많이 싸요.
I need to get travel insurance.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 짐 싸기: "Make a checklist." (체크리스트를 만들어요., 보통); "I always pack too much." (저는 늘 짐을 너무 많이 싸요., 보통); "Should I bring a ___?" (~ 가져가야 할까요?, 보통); "You won’t need it." (그건 필요 없을 거예요., 보통)
- 미리 챙기기: "I’d better charge my phone." (휴대폰 충전해 두는 게 좋겠어요., 보통); "Did you exchange money?" (환전했어요?, 보통); "I need to get travel insurance." (여행자 보험을 들어야 해요., 보통)
- 마무리 확인: "Is everything ready?" (다 준비됐어요?, 보통); "I think we’re all set." (다 된 것 같아요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 짐 낱말

*luggage* 짐(셀 수 없음): a lot of luggage · 하나씩은 a bag, a *suitcase*
*gear* = *equipment* 장비: camera gear
a *pair* of shoes 신발 한 켤레 · Can you *lift* it? 들 수 있어요?
돈과 보험

*exchange* money 환전하다 · *currency* 통화(나라의 돈)
*travel insurance* 여행자 보험(보장 범위는 보험사 최신 안내 확인)
(참고) *overseas* 해외의, 해외로: an overseas trip

A: Have you ___ your passport yet?   B: Not yet. It’s in the safe.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 짐 낱말: luggage 짐(셀 수 없음): a lot of luggage · 하나씩은 a bag, a suitcase / gear = equipment 장비: camera gear / a pair of shoes 신발 한 켤레 · Can you lift it? 들 수 있어요?
- 돈과 보험: exchange money 환전하다 · currency 통화(나라의 돈) / travel insurance 여행자 보험(보장 범위는 보험사 최신 안내 확인) / (참고) overseas 해외의, 해외로: an overseas trip
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Have you ___ your passport yet? B: Not yet. It’s in the safe. / A: Don’t ___ to take it out! B: I won’t. I’d ___ charge my phone, too. / A: Is everything ___? B: Yes. I think we’re all set. / 낱말 상자: packed · forget · better · ready
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: pack ((짐을) 싸다), suitcase (여행 가방), charger (충전기), adapter ((플러그) 어댑터), currency (통화(나라의 돈)), checklist (체크리스트, 확인 목록), toothbrush (칫솔), sunscreen (선크림), camera (카메라), equipment (장비), pair (한 쌍, 켤레), lift (들어 올리다).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: I always bring too much luggage.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: luggage (짐(셀 수 없음)) — "I always bring too much luggage."; bring (가져가다, 가져오다) — "Should I bring an umbrella?"; forget (잊다) — "Don’t forget to call me."; ready (준비된) — "Is everything ready?"; set (준비가 다 된(all set); 세트) — "I think we’re all set."; list (목록) — "Make a list."; exchange (바꾸다, 환전하다) — "I exchanged some money."; insurance (보험) — "travel insurance"; gear ((특정 활동용) 장비) — "camera gear"; overseas (해외의, 해외로) — "my first trip overseas".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Do you make a checklist before a trip?
Yes, I always make a checklist. / No, I just pack.
What do you sometimes forget to pack?
Your friend is going on a trip tomorrow. Tell them one thing.
Your phone is almost dead before a trip. What do you say?
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Do you make a checklist before a trip?" (hint on screen: Yes, I always make a checklist. / No, I just pack.)
- "What do you sometimes forget to pack?" (hint on screen: I sometimes forget my ___.)
- "Your friend is going on a trip tomorrow. Tell them one thing." (hint on screen: Don’t forget to ___!)
- "Your phone is almost dead before a trip. What do you say?" (hint on screen: I’d better charge my phone.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Packing Night
steps.text: It’s Jiwoo’s last night in Toronto. Tomorrow, she and Chloe *set out* for Chicago by train. Jiwoo makes a checklist: passport, charger, toothbrush, sunscreen, and a pair of comfortable shoes. It’s her first long trip overseas, so she checks everything twice. She needs neither a new adapter nor a bigger suitcase. Then Chloe sends a photo of her gear: two cameras and a big bag of equipment. She can hardly lift it all! “*In other words*, you’re bringing your whole office,” Jiwoo texts. Later, they check *one another’s* lists on the phone. Jiwoo keeps her cash and cards apart, in two different bags. That’s safe. Now she’s ready.
steps.gloss: set out 출발하다 · comfortable 편한 · neither A nor B A도 B도 아닌 · hardly 거의 ~ 못 하는 · in other words 다시 말해 · one another 서로 · apart 따로 떨어져
questions: What does Jiwoo put on her checklist?
Where does Jiwoo keep her cash and cards?

Reading on screen: "Packing Night". Text: "It’s Jiwoo’s last night in Toronto. Tomorrow, she and Chloe set out for Chicago by train. Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What does Jiwoo put on her checklist?" / "Where does Jiwoo keep her cash and cards?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘Have you packed ___ yet?’으로 짐을 챙겼는지 확인할 수 있어요.
‘Don’t forget to ___.’로 잊지 말라고 일러 줄 수 있어요.

Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘Have you packed ___ yet?’으로 짐을 챙겼는지 확인할 수 있어요.
- ‘Don’t forget to ___.’로 잊지 말라고 일러 줄 수 있어요.
- ‘I’d better ___.’로 미리 해 둘 일을 말할 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

lessons.title: 기차를 놓쳤어요
lessons.goal: 여행 중 문제를 말하고 다음 편을 묻고 표를 바꾸기

steps.title: 기차를 놓쳤어요
steps.goal: 여행 중 문제를 말하고 다음 편을 묻고 표를 바꾸기
steps.scene_desc: 5월 초 아침, 토론토의 큰 기차역 매표 창구 앞. 배낭을 멘 지우가 휴대폰을 귀에 댄 채 창구 직원(조연)에게 기차표를 내밀고, 뒤쪽 빈 승강장 너머로 멀어지는 기차가 보임(글자·간판 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "I missed my train." (기차를 놓쳤어요). Goal: 여행 중 문제를 말하고 다음 편을 묻고 표를 바꾸기. Today's scene: 5월 초 아침, 토론토의 큰 기차역 매표 창구 앞. 배낭을 멘 지우가 휴대폰을 귀에 댄 채 창구 직원에게 기차표를 내밀고, 뒤쪽 빈 승강장 너머로 멀어지는 기차가 보임. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Jiwoo, Chloe, Staff. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.

head: 무슨 일 (과거형)
다음 편 묻기
이어서 묻기
rows: I missed my train. 기차를 놓쳤어요.
My flight was canceled. 비행기 편이 취소됐어요.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: I missed my ___. When is the next ___? / Can I change my ticket? / Is there an extra charge? Table (무슨 일 (과거형) → 다음 편 묻기):
- I missed my train. 기차를 놓쳤어요. → When is the next train?
- My flight was canceled. 비행기 편이 취소됐어요. → When is the next flight?
- The bus was delayed. 버스가 늦어졌어요. → When is the next bus?
- I missed my ferry. 배를 놓쳤어요. → When is the next ferry?
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
이미 일어난 일은 과거형: I *missed* my train. 기차를 놓쳤어요.
‘~됐어요’는 *was* + -ed: The train *was delayed*. 늦어졌어요. · My flight *was canceled*. 취소됐어요.
canceled(미국) = cancelled(영국·캐나다)

When is *the next* train? 다음 기차는 언제예요?
Is there *an earlier* one? 더 이른 거 있어요? (one = train)
a *later* one 더 늦은 것 · the *last* train 마지막 기차
errors: 번호가 붙으면 platform 앞에 the 없이.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 과거형으로 일어난 일 말하기: 이미 일어난 일은 과거형: I missed my train. 기차를 놓쳤어요. / ‘~됐어요’는 was + -ed: The train was delayed. 늦어졌어요. · My flight was canceled. 취소됐어요. / canceled(미국) = cancelled(영국·캐나다)
- the next · an earlier one: When is the next train? 다음 기차는 언제예요? / Is there an earlier one? 더 이른 거 있어요? (one = train) / a later one 더 늦은 것 · the last train 마지막 기차
Common mistakes on screen:
- When is next train? → When is the next train? (‘다음 ~’는 the next.)
- The train was delay. → The train was delayed. (‘늦어졌다’는 was + delayed.)
- Is there a extra charge? → Is there an extra charge? (extra는 모음 소리로 시작해서 an.)
- It leaves from the platform 6. → It leaves from platform 6. (번호가 붙으면 platform 앞에 the 없이.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: 과거형으로 일어난 일 말하기: 이미 일어난 일은 과거형: I missed my train. 기차를 놓쳤어요.‘~됐어요’는 was + -ed: The train was delayed. 늦어졌어요. · My flight was canceled. 취소됐어요.canceled(미국) = cancelled(영국·캐나다)
the next · an earlier one: When is the next train? 다음 기차는 언제예요?Is there an earlier one? 더 이른 거 있어요? (one = train)a later one 더 늦은 것 · the last train 마지막 기차
mistakes: When is next train? → When is the next train?
The train was delay. → The train was delayed.
Is there a extra charge? → Is there an extra charge?
It leaves from the platform 6. → It leaves from platform 6.

steps.note: 예) train / 10:00 → I missed my train. When is the next train? — It’s at ten. · 선생님이 직원 역할로 대답해요.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) train / 10:00 → I missed my train. When is the next train? — It’s at ten. · 선생님이 직원 역할로 대답해요. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): train / 10:00 | bus / 1:30 | flight / 6:50 p.m. | ferry / 4:15.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "I missed my train." (기차를 놓쳤어요); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I missed my ___." / "When is the next ___?" / "Can I change my ticket?". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 문제 말하기: "My flight was canceled." (비행기 편이 취소됐어요., 보통); "The train was delayed." (기차가 늦어졌어요., 보통); "I’m in a hurry." (제가 좀 급해요., 보통); "What should I do now?" (이제 어떻게 해야 하죠?, 보통)
- 묻기: "Is there an earlier one?" (더 이른 거 있어요?, 보통); "Is there an extra charge?" (추가 요금이 있어요?, 정중); "Can I get a refund?" (환불받을 수 있어요?, 보통); "Is this seat taken?" (여기 자리 있어요?, 보통)
- 직원이 하는 말: "Let me check for you." (확인해 드릴게요., 정중); "It leaves from platform ___." (~번 승강장에서 출발해요., 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: platform · track · rail

미국에서는 타는 곳 번호를 *track*이라고도 해요: Track 6
travel by *rail* 기차로 여행하다 · the train *schedule* 기차 시간표
이 과의 기차 경로·시간·승강장·수수료는 연습용 가상 설정이에요. 실제 여행은 운영사의 최신 안내를 확인하세요.

a change *fee* 변경 수수료 · Can I get a *refund*? 환불돼요?

Tips on screen:

Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.

Picture words on screen. New: platform (승강장, 타는 곳), track (선로; (미국) 타는 곳), rail (철도, 레일), vehicle (차량, 탈것), speed (속도), license (면허증), departure (출발), arrival (도착), transfer (갈아타기; 갈아타다), schedule (시간표, 일정), ticket counter (매표소), restroom (화장실).

Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.

Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: The Ten O’Clock Train
steps.text: At 9:45, Jiwoo went down to platform 6. This time, she didn’t *go into* any shops or restrooms! The doors closed, and soon the train picked up speed. Jiwoo walked the whole length of the train to the café car. A big bag was *in the way*, so she asked an older man, “Excuse me, is this seat taken?” He smiled and moved his bag. Then he *laid out* a paper map on the table and showed her the stops. “Just relax and enjoy the view,” he said. Jiwoo sent Chloe a message: “I *wound up* on a later train, but I have a window seat and a new friend. See you in Chicago!”
steps.gloss: go into ~에 들어가다 · pick up speed 속도를 내다 · walk the length of ~의 끝에서 끝까지 걷다(length 길이) · café car 기차의 식당 칸 · in the way 길을 막는, 방해가 되는 · lay out 펼쳐 놓다(laid는 과거형) · wind up 결국 ~하게 되다(wound는 과거형)
questions: What was in the way in the café car?
What did Jiwoo write to Chloe?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "The Ten O’Clock Train". Text: "At 9:45, Jiwoo went down to platform 6. This time, she didn’t go into any shops or restrooms! The doors closed, and soon the train picked up speed. Jiwoo walked the whole length of the train to the café car. A big bag was in the way, so she asked an older man, “Excuse me, is this seat taken?” He smiled and moved his bag. Then he laid out a paper map on the table and showed her the stops. “Just relax and enjoy the view,” he said. Jiwoo sent Chloe a message: “I wound up on a later train, but I have a window seat and a new friend. See you in Chicago!”" Words: go into ~에 들어가다 · pick up speed 속도를 내다 · walk the length of ~의 끝에서 끝까지 걷다(length 길이) · café car 기차의 식당 칸 · in the way 길을 막는, 방해가 되는 · lay out 펼쳐 놓다(laid는 과거형) · wind up 결국 ~하게 되다(wound는 과거형).
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What was in the way in the café car?" / "What did Jiwoo write to Chloe?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.

Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. steps.title: 길을 잃었어요
steps.goal: 길을 잃었다고 말하고 지도로 위치를 확인하기
steps.scene_desc: 5월 초 저녁, 시카고의 큰 기차역 근처 좁은 길. 배낭을 멘 지우가 휴대폰을 내밀고, 지나가던 사람(조연)이 휴대폰 지도를 손가락으로 가리켜 줌. 길 끝으로 강과 다리, 회색 탑 건물이 보임(글자·간판 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "I think I’m lost." (길을 잃었어요). Goal: 길을 잃었다고 말하고 지도로 위치를 확인하기. Today's scene: 5월 초 저녁, 시카고의 큰 기차역 근처 좁은 길. 배낭을 멘 지우가 휴대폰을 내밀고, 지나가던 사람이 휴대폰 지도를 손가락으로 가리켜 줌. 길 끝으로 강과 다리, 회색 탑 건물이 보임. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Jiwoo, Daniel, Passerby. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I think I’m lost.".

steps.when: 낯선 곳에서 길을 모를 때 먼저 하는 말이에요. lost = 길을 잃은.
steps.extra: I think I’m lost. I’m trying to get to the station.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I think I’m lost." (길을 잃은 것 같아요.). When to use it: 낯선 곳에서 길을 모를 때 먼저 하는 말이에요. lost = 길을 잃은. Note: I think I’m lost. I’m trying to get to the station.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Could you show me on the map?".

steps.title: Which Way? · 시카고에 도착한 저녁, 큰 역 근처에서

lines.en: Daniel, it’s me. {{I think I’m lost}}.
lines.ko: 대니얼, 저예요. 길을 잃은 것 같아요.

lines.en: Don’t panic. Chloe and I are at a gas station near the square. Can you see any landmarks?
lines.ko: 당황하지 마요. 클로이랑 저는 광장 근처 주유소에 있어요. 눈에 띄는 건물 같은 게 보여요?

lines.en: A gray tower and the river. The bridge on my map was shut down, so I went another way.
lines.ko: 회색 탑이랑 강이요. 지도에 나온 다리가 막혀서 다른 길로 갔어요.

lines.en: Okay. Ask someone nearby. See you at Willow Square!
lines.ko: 알았어요. 근처 사람한테 물어봐요. 윌로 광장에서 만나요!

lines.en: Excuse me. I’m trying to get to Willow Square. Am I going the right way?
lines.ko: 실례합니다. 윌로 광장에 가려고 하는데요. 이 길이 맞아요?

lines.en: Hmm, you’re going the wrong way. Go back the way you came.
lines.ko: 음, 반대로 가고 계세요. 오신 길로 돌아가세요.

lines.en: {{Could you show me on the map}}?
lines.ko: 지도에서 좀 보여 주시겠어요?

lines.en: Sure. We’re here, and the square is up here, to the north. Turn left onto the broad street at the next intersection.
lines.ko: 그럼요. 우리는 여기, 광장은 위쪽 북쪽이에요. 다음 교차로에서 왼쪽으로 돌아 넓은 길로 들어가세요.

lines.en: {{Is it within walking distance}}?
lines.ko: 걸어갈 만한 거리예요?

lines.en: Yes, it’s about ten minutes on foot. Actually, I’m going that way. I’ll walk you there.
lines.ko: 네, 걸어서 10분쯤이에요. 실은 저도 그쪽으로 가요. 거기까지 같이 가 드릴게요.

lines.en: Thanks, you’re a lifesaver!
lines.ko: 고마워요, 정말 살았어요!

steps.teach:

Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: I think I’m lost. I’m trying to get to ___. / Could you show me on the map? / Is it within walking distance? Table (가려는 곳 → 이렇게 물어요):
- the station 역 → Which way is the station?
- the bridge 다리 → Could you show me on the map?
- the museum 박물관 → Is it within walking distance?
- the airport 공항 → Is it within walking distance?
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
공손한 부탁은 *Could you* + 동사원형: *Could you show me* on the map? 지도에서 좀 보여 주시겠어요?
Could you show me *the way* to the station? 역 가는 길 좀 알려 주시겠어요?

Is it *within walking distance*? 걸어갈 만한 거리예요?
It’s about ten minutes *on foot*. 걸어서 10분쯤이에요.
I’m *trying to get to* the square. 광장에 가려고 하는데요.
errors: Could you showing me the way?
Could you show me the way?
Could you show me on map?
Could you show me on the map?
지금 보는 지도라 map 앞에 the.
I’m trying to get the station.
I’m trying to get to the station.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- Could you show me ~?: 공손한 부탁은 Could you + 동사원형: Could you show me on the map? 지도에서 좀 보여 주시겠어요? / Could you show me the way to the station? 역 가는 길 좀 알려 주시겠어요?
- 거리 묻고 말하기: Is it within walking distance? 걸어갈 만한 거리예요? / It’s about ten minutes on foot. 걸어서 10분쯤이에요. / I’m trying to get to the square. 광장에 가려고 하는데요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Could you showing me the way? → Could you show me the way? (Could you 뒤에는 동사원형.)
- Could you show me on map? → Could you show me on the map? (지금 보는 지도라 map 앞에 the.)
- Is it within walk distance? → Is it within walking distance? (‘걸어갈 거리’는 walking distance.)
- I’m trying to get the station. → I’m trying to get to the station. (‘~에 가다’는 get to + 장소.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) Willow Square / ten minutes on foot → I’m trying to get to Willow Square. Is it within walking distance? — Yes, it’s about ten minutes on foot.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) Willow Square / ten minutes on foot → I’m trying to get to Willow Square. Is it within walking distance? — Yes, it’s about ten minutes on foot. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): Willow Square / ten minutes on foot | the station / five minutes on foot | the museum / twenty minutes on foot | the airport / take a taxi.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: Could you show me on the map?
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "I think I’m lost." (길을 잃었어요); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I think I’m lost." / "Could you show me on the map?" / "Is it within walking distance?". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Am I going the right way?
Go back the way you came.
It’s about ten minutes on foot.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 길을 잃었을 때: "I’m trying to get to ___." (~에 가려고 하는데요., 보통); "Which way is ___?" (~는 어느 쪽이에요?, 보통); "Am I going the right way?" (이 길이 맞아요?, 보통)
- 길 알려 주기: "You’re going the wrong way." (반대로 가고 계세요., 보통); "Go back the way you came." (오신 길로 돌아가세요., 보통); "It’s about ten minutes on foot." (걸어서 10분쯤이에요., 보통); "You’d better take a taxi." (택시를 타는 게 좋겠어요., 보통)
- 도움 주고받기: "I’ll walk you there." (거기까지 같이 가 드릴게요., 친근); "Thanks, you’re a lifesaver." (고마워요, 정말 살았어요., 친근); "Don’t panic." (당황하지 마요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 동서남북 · 방향

Walk *north* along the river. 강을 따라 북쪽으로 걸어요.
It’s *directly* across from the station. 역 바로 맞은편이에요.

길 사정 말하기

The bridge is closed for *construction*. 다리가 공사로 막혔어요.
a *narrow* street 좁은 길 ↔ a *broad* street 넓은 길
Turn left *onto* the broad street. 왼쪽으로 돌아 넓은 길로 들어가요.
Let’s take a different *route*. 다른 길로 가요.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 동서남북 · 방향: north 북 · south 남 · east 동 · west 서 / Walk north along the river. 강을 따라 북쪽으로 걸어요. / It’s directly across from the station. 역 바로 맞은편이에요. / I went in the wrong direction. 엉뚱한 방향으로 갔어요.
- 길 사정 말하기: The bridge is closed for construction. 다리가 공사로 막혔어요. / a narrow street 좁은 길 ↔ a broad street 넓은 길 / Turn left onto the broad street. 왼쪽으로 돌아 넓은 길로 들어가요. / Let’s take a different route. 다른 길로 가요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Excuse me. I think I’m ___. Could you ___ me on the map? B: Sure. You’re going the ___ way. / A: Is it within walking ___? B: Yes, it’s about ten minutes on ___. / 낱말 상자: lost · show · wrong · distance · foot
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: north (북쪽), south (남쪽), east (동쪽), west (서쪽), foot (발(on foot 걸어서)), landmark (랜드마크, 눈에 띄는 건물), intersection (교차로), bridge (다리), square (광장), construction (공사), map (지도), sign (표지판).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

steps.title: The Long Way to Willow Square
steps.text: Daniel’s plan was simple. “The square is *no more than* ten minutes from the station. It’s easy!” But the bridge on Jiwoo’s route was *shut down* for construction, and her map app didn’t *take into account* the closed bridge. So Jiwoo walked in the wrong direction, into a narrow street in an old district. At the same time, Daniel and Chloe were at a gas station. The car’s tank was almost empty! In the end, a kind stranger walked Jiwoo to the square. Daniel laughed and gave her a big hug. “Sorry, Jiwoo. I said it was easy. I *take back* what I said!” Then Chloe handed Jiwoo her suitcase. “Here you go, safe and sound!”

questions: Why did Jiwoo walk in the wrong direction?
Where were Daniel and Chloe at the same time?

steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "What’s in it?" (현지 음식). Goal: 처음 보는 음식의 재료와 맛을 묻고 말하기. Today's scene: 5월 초 저녁, 시카고 동네 식당 테이블. 지우·대니얼·클로이가 둘러앉고, 대니얼이 두툼한 딥디시 피자 한 조각을 들어 보이며 설명하고, 지우는 포크를 든 채 신기한 얼굴로 봄. 테이블에는 초록색 수프도 놓여 있음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Daniel, Jiwoo, Chloe. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). (1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).

steps.title: Deep-Dish Pizza · 5월 초 저녁, 시카고 동네 식당에서

lines.en: Let’s go over the menu. I always get the chicken breast sandwich, but try the pizza.

lines.ko: 좋아요! 솔직히 생각보다 더 맛있어요.

steps.teach:

1. Daniel: "Let’s go over the menu. I always get the chicken breast sandwich, but try the pizza." (메뉴 훑어봐요. 저는 늘 닭가슴살 샌드위치지만, 피자를 먹어 봐요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Deep-dish pizza? What’s in it?" (딥디시 피자요? 뭐가 들어 있어요?)
3. Daniel: "It’s made with lots of cheese and tomato sauce. It’s a regional dish, so it’s rare outside Chicago." (치즈를 듬뿍 넣고 토마토소스로 만들어요. 이 지역 요리라서 시카고 밖에서는 보기 드물어요.)
4. Chloe: "Ooh! And this green soup? Is it vegetarian?" (오! 그럼 이 초록색 수프는요? 채식이에요?)
5. Daniel: "Yes. It’s made with fresh spinach and local corn." (네. 신선한 시금치와 이 지역 옥수수로 만들어요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Here’s our pizza! Wow, it smells amazing. Is it spicy?" (피자 나왔다! 와, 냄새 끝내줘요. 매워요?)
7. Daniel: "Not at all. The sauce is a little sweet. Go ahead, try some." (전혀요. 소스가 조금 달아요. 어서 먹어 봐요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Mmm! It tastes a bit like a pie, and it’s so soft inside. Why is it so good?" (음! 맛이 좀 파이 같고, 속이 정말 부드러워요. 왜 이렇게 맛있어요?)

10. Chloe: "Recipes vary from family to family, right, Daniel?" (요리법은 집집마다 다르죠, 대니얼?)
11. Daniel: "Right. My mom makes her own version. You should try it someday!" (맞아요. 우리 엄마도 엄마만의 방식으로 만들어요. 언젠가 꼭 먹어 봐요!)
12. Jiwoo: "I’d love to! Honestly, it’s better than I expected." (좋아요! 솔직히 생각보다 더 맛있어요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
