First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Daniel and Chloe. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: Deep-dish pizza is rare outside Chicago.
The green soup is made with meat.
steps.teach:
True/false check. The statements on the learner's screen, each with its answer and the scene line that shows it. The answers are for you only: never say an answer or a line number before the learner has answered:
1. Deep-dish pizza is rare outside Chicago. → True (line 3)
2. The green soup is made with meat. → False (line 4, 5)
3. Jiwoo doesn’t like the pizza. → False (line 8, 12)
The scene they are about:
1. Daniel: "Let’s go over the menu. I always get the chicken breast sandwich, but try the pizza." (메뉴 훑어봐요. 저는 늘 닭가슴살 샌드위치지만, 피자를 먹어 봐요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Deep-dish pizza? What’s in it?" (딥디시 피자요? 뭐가 들어 있어요?)
3. Daniel: "It’s made with lots of cheese and tomato sauce. It’s a regional dish, so it’s rare outside Chicago." (치즈를 듬뿍 넣고 토마토소스로 만들어요. 이 지역 요리라서 시카고 밖에서는 보기 드물어요.)
4. Chloe: "Ooh! And this green soup? Is it vegetarian?" (오! 그럼 이 초록색 수프는요? 채식이에요?)
5. Daniel: "Yes. It’s made with fresh spinach and local corn." (네. 신선한 시금치와 이 지역 옥수수로 만들어요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Here’s our pizza! Wow, it smells amazing. Is it spicy?" (피자 나왔다! 와, 냄새 끝내줘요. 매워요?)
7. Daniel: "Not at all. The sauce is a little sweet. Go ahead, try some." (전혀요. 소스가 조금 달아요. 어서 먹어 봐요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Mmm! It tastes a bit like a pie, and it’s so soft inside. Why is it so good?" (음! 맛이 좀 파이 같고, 속이 정말 부드러워요. 왜 이렇게 맛있어요?)
9. Daniel: "Here’s why. The sauce cooks for hours, so the flavor is complex." (이유는 이거예요. 소스를 몇 시간 끓여서 맛이 깊고 풍부해요.)
10. Chloe: "Recipes vary from family to family, right, Daniel?" (요리법은 집집마다 다르죠, 대니얼?)
11. Daniel: "Right. My mom makes her own version. You should try it someday!" (맞아요. 우리 엄마도 엄마만의 방식으로 만들어요. 언젠가 꼭 먹어 봐요!)
12. Jiwoo: "I’d love to! Honestly, it’s better than I expected." (좋아요! 솔직히 생각보다 더 맛있어요.)
Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: It’s made with ___. It tastes a bit like ___.
head: 음식
재료 말하기 (made with)
맛 말하기
rows: It’s made with cheese and tomato sauce.
It tastes a bit like a pie.
It’s made with spinach and corn.
It tastes a bit like cake.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: What’s in it? / Is it ___? / It’s made with ___. It tastes a bit like ___. Table (음식 → 재료 말하기 (made with)):
- deep-dish pizza 딥디시 피자 → It’s made with cheese and tomato sauce.
- green soup 초록색 수프 → It’s made with spinach and corn.
- cornbread 옥수수빵 → It’s made with corn.
- hot sauce 매운 소스 → It’s made with red peppers.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
It’s *made with* cheese and tomato sauce. 치즈와 토마토소스로 만들어요.
재료(ingredients)를 물을 때: What’s in it? = What’s it made with?
It’s는 It is. made with 앞의 is를 빼지 않아요.

맛 형용사는 바로: It *tastes sweet*. 달아요.
아는 음식에 빗댈 때는 like: It *tastes like* a pie. 파이 같은 맛이에요.
‘조금’은 *a bit · a little*: It tastes a bit like a pie.
errors: It tastes a bit like chicken.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- be made with + 재료: It’s made with cheese and tomato sauce. 치즈와 토마토소스로 만들어요. / 재료(ingredients)를 물을 때: What’s in it? = What’s it made with? / It’s는 It is. made with 앞의 is를 빼지 않아요.
- taste + 형용사 · taste like + 명사: 맛 형용사는 바로: It tastes sweet. 달아요. / 아는 음식에 빗댈 때는 like: It tastes like a pie. 파이 같은 맛이에요. / ‘조금’은 a bit · a little: It tastes a bit like a pie.
Common mistakes on screen:
- It tastes like sweet. → It tastes sweet. (맛 형용사(sweet) 앞에는 like 없이.)
- It’s made by cheese. → It’s made with cheese. (재료를 말할 때는 made with.)
- It tastes a bit chicken. → It tastes a bit like chicken. (음식 이름(명사) 앞에는 like.)
- I’m allergy to nuts. → I’m allergic to nuts. (‘알레르기가 있는’은 allergic.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: be made with + 재료: It’s made with cheese and tomato sauce. 치즈와 토마토소스로 만들어요.재료(ingredients)를 물을 때: What’s in it? = What’s it made with?It’s는 It is. made with 앞의 is를 빼지 않아요.
taste + 형용사 · taste like + 명사: 맛 형용사는 바로: It tastes sweet. 달아요.아는 음식에 빗댈 때는 like: It tastes like a pie. 파이 같은 맛이에요.‘조금’은 a bit · a little: It tastes a bit like a pie.
mistakes: It tastes like sweet. → It tastes sweet.
It’s made by cheese. → It’s made with cheese.
It tastes a bit chicken. → It tastes a bit like chicken.
I’m allergy to nuts. → I’m allergic to nuts.

steps.note: 예) deep-dish pizza / cheese · a pie → What’s in it? — It’s made with cheese. It tastes a bit like a pie.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) deep-dish pizza / cheese · a pie → What’s in it? — It’s made with cheese. It tastes a bit like a pie. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): deep-dish pizza / cheese · a pie | this cornbread / corn · cake | this sauce / honey · candy | this drink / ginger · tea.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "What’s in it?" (현지 음식); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What’s in it?" / "It’s made with ___." / "It tastes a bit like ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Do you want to try some?
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 맛 묻고 말하기: "Is it spicy?" (매워요?, 보통); "It’s a little sweet." (조금 달아요., 보통); "It’s too salty for me." (저한테는 너무 짜요., 보통); "This is so good!" (이거 진짜 맛있어요!, 친근)
- 권하고 먹어 보기: "Do you want to try some?" (좀 먹어 볼래요?, 친근); "I’ll give it a try." (한번 먹어 볼게요., 보통); "It’s better than I expected." (생각보다 더 맛있어요., 보통)
- 주문할 때 확인하기: "I’m allergic to ___." (저는 ~ 알레르기가 있어요., 보통); "Is it vegetarian?" (채식 요리예요?, 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 맛을 말하는 낱말

*sweet* 단 · *salty* 짠 · *sour* 신 · *bitter* 쓴 · *spicy* 매운
a rich, *complex* *flavor* 여러 맛이 어우러진 깊은 맛
It’s *soft* inside. 속이 부드러워요.
look · smell · taste

It *looks* good. 맛있어 보여요. · It *smells* amazing. 냄새가 끝내줘요.
It *tastes like* chicken. 닭고기 같은 맛이 나요.
Recipes *vary*. 요리법은 집마다·가게마다 달라요.
steps.blank:
A: What’s ___ it?   B: It’s made ___ cheese and tomato sauce.
A: Is it spicy?   B: No. It tastes a bit ___ a pie.
A: Mmm! It’s ___ than I expected.
낱말 상자: in · with · like · better
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 맛을 말하는 낱말: sweet 단 · salty 짠 · sour 신 · bitter 쓴 · spicy 매운 / a rich, complex flavor 여러 맛이 어우러진 깊은 맛 / It’s soft inside. 속이 부드러워요.
- look · smell · taste: It looks good. 맛있어 보여요. · It smells amazing. 냄새가 끝내줘요. / It tastes like chicken. 닭고기 같은 맛이 나요. / Recipes vary. 요리법은 집마다·가게마다 달라요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: What’s ___ it? B: It’s made ___ cheese and tomato sauce. / A: Is it spicy? B: No. It tastes a bit ___ a pie. / A: Mmm! It’s ___ than I expected. / 낱말 상자: in · with · like · better
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: taste (맛; 맛보다), sweet (단, 달콤한), salty (짠), sour (신, 시큼한), bitter (쓴), fresh (신선한), sauce (소스), ingredient (재료), recipe (요리법, 레시피), produce (농산물(채소·과일)), wine (와인, 포도주), sample (시식품, 맛보기).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: The flavor is rich and complex.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: flavor (맛, 풍미) — "The flavor is rich and complex."; vegetarian (채식의; 채식주의자) — "Is this soup vegetarian?"; allergic (알레르기가 있는) — "I’m allergic to nuts."; expect (예상하다, 기대하다) — "It’s better than I expected."; spicy (매운) — "Is it spicy?"; dish (요리, 음식) — "a regional dish"; local (그 지역의, 현지의) — "fresh local corn"; regional (지역의, 그 지방의) — "It’s a regional dish."; rare (드문, 보기 힘든) — "It’s rare outside Chicago."; variety (여러 가지, 다양함) — "a wide variety of fruit".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

steps.role: *역할 카드*의 가상 손님으로 답해요: 견과류 알레르기가 있고, 고기를 먹지 않아요.
items: I work at this restaurant. Do you have any allergies? (역할 카드)
Our chicken soup is very popular today. (역할 카드)
Sorry, I don’t eat meat. Is the green soup vegetarian?
What’s a Korean dish you love? What’s in it?
Think of a new food you tried. What did it taste like?
It tasted a bit like ___. It was better than I expected.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "I work at this restaurant. Do you have any allergies? (역할 카드)" (hint on screen: Yes. I’m allergic to nuts.)
- "Our chicken soup is very popular today. (역할 카드)" (hint on screen: Sorry, I don’t eat meat. Is the green soup vegetarian?)
- "What’s a Korean dish you love? What’s in it?" (hint on screen: I love ___. It’s made with ___.)
- "Think of a new food you tried. What did it taste like?" (hint on screen: It tasted a bit like ___. It was better than I expected.)
Role card on screen (the learner may answer as this role): 역할 카드의 가상 손님으로 답해요: 견과류 알레르기가 있고, 고기를 먹지 않아요.
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: I work at this restaurant. Do you have any allergies? (역할 카드)
Our chicken soup is very popular today. (역할 카드)
What’s a Korean dish you love? What’s in it?

steps.title: A Morning at the Market
steps.text: The next morning, Daniel takes Jiwoo and Chloe to a farmers market near his parents’ house. There is a wide variety of fresh local produce, and many stands give out free samples. Jiwoo tries a green pickle. It’s very sour! The dark chocolate is a little bitter, but she likes it. Chloe buys a jar of honey, and Daniel chooses a bottle of local wine for his parents. At the last stand, a man sells his *so-called* “world’s best” hot sauce. Jiwoo tries some and drinks a lot of water. Daniel laughs. “It hurts *in the short term*, but tomorrow you’ll want more.”
steps.gloss: farmers market 농산물 시장 · stand 가판대 · give out 나눠 주다 · jar 병 · so-called(so called) 이른바 · in the short term 당장은
questions: What does Daniel buy for his parents?
Why does Jiwoo drink water?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "A Morning at the Market". Text: "The next morning, Daniel takes Jiwoo and Chloe to a farmers market near his parents’ house. There is a wide variety of fresh local produce, and many stands give out free samples. Jiwoo tries a green pickle. It’s very sour! The dark chocolate is a little bitter, but she likes it. Chloe buys a jar of honey, and Daniel chooses a bottle of local wine for his parents. At the last stand, a man sells his so-called “world’s best” hot sauce. Jiwoo tries some and drinks a lot of water. Daniel laughs. “It hurts in the short term, but tomorrow you’ll want more.”" Words: farmers market 농산물 시장 · stand 가판대 · give out 나눠 주다 · jar 병 · so-called(so called) 이른바 · in the short term 당장은.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What does Daniel buy for his parents?" / "Why does Jiwoo drink water?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘What’s in it?’으로 처음 보는 음식의 재료를 물을 수 있어요.
‘It’s made with ___.’로 음식이 무엇으로 만들어졌는지 말할 수 있어요.
‘It tastes a bit like ___.’로 아는 맛에 빗대어 맛을 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘What’s in it?’으로 처음 보는 음식의 재료를 물을 수 있어요.
- ‘It’s made with ___.’로 음식이 무엇으로 만들어졌는지 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘It tastes a bit like ___.’로 아는 맛에 빗대어 맛을 말할 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 여기 좀 봐요
steps.title_en: This is where the boat tours start.
steps.goal: 사진 속 장소를 소개하고 꼭 할 일을 권하기
steps.scene_desc: 5월 초 오후, 시카고 강가 산책로. 높은 건물들 사이로 강이 흐르고, 강 건너편에 오래된 돌 극장 건물이 보임. 클로이가 강 쪽을 손으로 가리키고, 지우가 휴대폰을 가로로 들고 사진을 찍음(간판·글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "This is where the boat tours start." (여기 좀 봐요). Goal: 사진 속 장소를 소개하고 꼭 할 일을 권하기. Today's scene: 5월 초 오후, 시카고 강가 산책로. 높은 건물들 사이로 강이 흐르고, 강 건너편에 오래된 돌 극장 건물이 보임. 클로이가 강 쪽을 손으로 가리키고, 지우가 휴대폰을 가로로 들고 사진을 찍음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Chloe, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: This is where ___. / It’s famous for ___. You should definitely ___. Table (장소 → 소개하기 (This is where …)):

- the theater 극장 → This is where people see shows.
- the lake 호수 → This is where we watched the sunset.
- the tower 타워 → This is where I took this photo.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.

items:
This is *where* the boat tours *start*. 여기가 보트 투어가 출발하는 곳이에요.
where 뒤는 *주어 + 동사*: where we watched the sunset

It’s *famous for* its buildings. 건물로 유명해요.
for 뒤에는 명사나 -ing: famous for deep-dish pizza
꼭 해 보라고 권할 때: You *should definitely* go.

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- This is where + 주어 + 동사: This is where the boat tours start. 여기가 보트 투어가 출발하는 곳이에요. / where 뒤는 주어 + 동사: where we watched the sunset
- be famous for · should definitely: It’s famous for its buildings. 건물로 유명해요. / for 뒤에는 명사나 -ing: famous for deep-dish pizza / 꼭 해 보라고 권할 때: You should definitely go.
Common mistakes on screen:
- This is where start the boat tours. → This is where the boat tours start. (where 뒤에는 주어 + 동사.)
- The city is famous with its buildings. → The city is famous for its buildings. (‘~로 유명한’은 famous for.)
- This is the place I told you. → This is the place I told you about. (‘~에 대해’ 말한 곳이라 about을 붙여요.)
- It was packed of tourists. → It was packed with tourists. (‘~로 꽉 찬’은 packed with.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:

When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.

If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "This is where the boat tours start." (여기 좀 봐요); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "This is where ___." / "It’s famous for ___." / "You should definitely ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: This is the place I told you about.
We got there just before sunset.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 사진 보여 주며 소개하기: "Look at this!" (이거 봐요!, 친근); "Here’s a picture of ___." (이게 ~ 사진이에요., 보통); "This is the place I told you about." (전에 말한 데가 여기예요., 보통)
- 감탄하기: "Isn’t it gorgeous?" (정말 멋지지 않아요?, 친근); "The view was breathtaking." (경치가 숨 막히게 멋졌어요., 보통); "It’s a must-see." (꼭 봐야 할 곳이에요., 보통)

Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Photos from the Lake
steps.text: In the evening, Jiwoo and Chloe take the boat tour. It’s a popular attraction, so the boat is packed with tourists. Small flags wave in the wind. The guide talks about the city’s history. “This river is a symbol of the city. Its beauty attracts millions of visitors.” After the tour, they walk to the lake. It’s vast, like the sea, and the waves are powerful. They get there just before sunset. What a sight! Jiwoo takes a photograph of the lake under the colorful evening sky. The wind is cold, but she doesn’t want to leave. She *keeps in touch with* Grace in Seoul, so she sends the photo right away: “Here’s a picture of the lake. Isn’t it gorgeous? I wish you were here!”
steps.gloss: attraction 명소 · wave 흔들리다; 파도 · symbol 상징 · beauty 아름다움 · attract 끌다 · vast 광대한 · powerful 강한 · sight 광경 · keep in touch with ~와 연락하다

Who does Jiwoo send the picture to?

lessons.title: 약국에서

steps.title: 약국에서
steps.title_en: I’ve had a sore throat since yesterday.
steps.goal: 몸 상태와 기간을 말하고 약 먹는 법을 묻기
steps.scene_desc: 5월 초 오전, 시카고의 동네 약국 안쪽 계산대. 목도리를 두른 지우가 목을 가리키며 약사(조연)에게 설명하고, 옆에서 대니얼이 걱정스러운 얼굴로 지켜봄(상자·선반·간판에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "I’ve had a sore throat since yesterday." (약국에서). Goal: 몸 상태와 기간을 말하고 약 먹는 법을 묻기. Today's scene: 5월 초 오전, 시카고의 동네 약국 안쪽 계산대. 목도리를 두른 지우가 목을 가리키며 약사에게 설명하고, 옆에서 대니얼이 걱정스러운 얼굴로 지켜봄. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Daniel, Jiwoo, Staff. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I don’t feel well.".

steps.when: 약국·병원에서 먼저 꺼내는 말이에요. 그다음에 어디가 어떤지 말해요.
steps.extra: I don’t feel well. I have a sore throat.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I don’t feel well." (몸이 좀 안 좋아요.). When to use it: 약국·병원에서 먼저 꺼내는 말이에요. 그다음에 어디가 어떤지 말해요. Note: I don’t feel well. I have a sore throat.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I’ve had a ___ since ___.".

steps.when: 증상이 언제 시작돼 지금까지 이어지는지 말해요. have의 현재완료 *’ve had* + since 시작한 때.
steps.extra: I’ve had a cough since Monday. · I’ve had a cold for two days.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I’ve had a ___ since ___." (~부터 (지금까지) ~가 있어요.). When to use it: 증상이 언제 시작돼 지금까지 이어지는지 말해요. have의 현재완료 ’ve had + since 시작한 때. Note: I’ve had a cough since Monday. · I’ve had a cold for two days.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "How often should I take it?".

Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("At the Pharmacy · 시카고의 아침, 동네 약국에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: At the Pharmacy · 시카고의 아침, 동네 약국에서

lines.en: You don’t look great, Jiwoo. Are you okay?
lines.ko: 지우 씨, 안색이 안 좋네요. 괜찮아요?

lines.en: Not really. {{I don’t feel well}}. {{I’ve had a}} sore throat {{since}} yesterday.
lines.ko: 별로요. 몸이 안 좋아요. 어제부터 목이 아파요.

lines.en: They say the pharmacy on the corner is good. Let’s go.
lines.ko: 모퉁이 약국이 괜찮다던데요. 가 봐요.

lines.en: Hi there. What are your symptoms?
lines.ko: 안녕하세요. 어떤 증상이 있으세요?

lines.en: I’ve got a runny nose, and I can’t stop coughing.
lines.ko: 콧물이 나고, 기침이 멈추질 않아요.

lines.en: How long have you had the cough?
lines.ko: 기침은 얼마나 됐어요?

lines.en: {{Since}} last night. Do I need a prescription?
lines.ko: 어젯밤부터요. 처방전이 필요해요?

lines.en: No. This one is for colds. Do you have any allergies?
lines.ko: 아뇨. 이건 감기약이에요. 알레르기 있어요?

lines.en: No. {{How often should I take it}}?
lines.ko: 없어요. 얼마나 자주 먹어야 해요?

lines.en: Follow the directions on the box. Let me show you.
lines.ko: 상자의 안내대로 드세요. 제가 보여 드릴게요.

lines.en: Are there any side effects?

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "At the Pharmacy · 시카고의 아침, 동네 약국에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Daniel: "You don’t look great, Jiwoo. Are you okay?" (지우 씨, 안색이 안 좋네요. 괜찮아요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Not really. I don’t feel well. I’ve had a sore throat since yesterday." (별로요. 몸이 안 좋아요. 어제부터 목이 아파요.)
3. Daniel: "They say the pharmacy on the corner is good. Let’s go." (모퉁이 약국이 괜찮다던데요. 가 봐요.)
4. Staff: "Hi there. What are your symptoms?" (안녕하세요. 어떤 증상이 있으세요?)
5. Jiwoo: "I’ve got a runny nose, and I can’t stop coughing." (콧물이 나고, 기침이 멈추질 않아요.)
6. Staff: "How long have you had the cough?" (기침은 얼마나 됐어요?)
7. Jiwoo: "Since last night. Do I need a prescription?" (어젯밤부터요. 처방전이 필요해요?)
8. Staff: "No. This one is for colds. Do you have any allergies?" (아뇨. 이건 감기약이에요. 알레르기 있어요?)
9. Jiwoo: "No. How often should I take it?" (없어요. 얼마나 자주 먹어야 해요?)
10. Staff: "Follow the directions on the box. Let me show you." (상자의 안내대로 드세요. 제가 보여 드릴게요.)
11. Daniel: "Are there any side effects?" (부작용은 있어요?)
12. Staff: "It might make you sleepy. If it gets worse, see a doctor. I hope you feel better!" (졸릴 수 있어요. 더 나빠지면 병원에 가 보세요. 빨리 나으세요!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

steps.teach:
Role reading of the same scene. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Daniel, Staff exactly as written, word for word. Never change, add or skip a line, and never read the learner's lines for them first.
1. Daniel (you): "You don’t look great, Jiwoo. Are you okay?" (지우 씨, 안색이 안 좋네요. 괜찮아요?)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "Not really. I don’t feel well. I’ve had a sore throat since yesterday." (별로요. 몸이 안 좋아요. 어제부터 목이 아파요.)
3. Daniel (you): "They say the pharmacy on the corner is good. Let’s go." (모퉁이 약국이 괜찮다던데요. 가 봐요.)
4. Staff (you): "Hi there. What are your symptoms?" (안녕하세요. 어떤 증상이 있으세요?)
5. Jiwoo (learner): "I’ve got a runny nose, and I can’t stop coughing." (콧물이 나고, 기침이 멈추질 않아요.)
6. Staff (you): "How long have you had the cough?" (기침은 얼마나 됐어요?)
7. Jiwoo (learner): "Since last night. Do I need a prescription?" (어젯밤부터요. 처방전이 필요해요?)
8. Staff (you): "No. This one is for colds. Do you have any allergies?" (아뇨. 이건 감기약이에요. 알레르기 있어요?)
9. Jiwoo (learner): "No. How often should I take it?" (없어요. 얼마나 자주 먹어야 해요?)
10. Staff (you): "Follow the directions on the box. Let me show you." (상자의 안내대로 드세요. 제가 보여 드릴게요.)
11. Daniel (you): "Are there any side effects?" (부작용은 있어요?)
12. Staff (you): "It might make you sleepy. If it gets worse, see a doctor. I hope you feel better!" (졸릴 수 있어요. 더 나빠지면 병원에 가 보세요. 빨리 나으세요!)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Daniel and Staff. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

frame: I don’t feel well. I’ve had a ___ since ___.
How often should I take it? / Do I need a prescription?
head: 증상
since + 시작한 때
for + 기간
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: I don’t feel well. I’ve had a ___ since ___. / How often should I take it? / Do I need a prescription? Table (증상 → since + 시작한 때):
- a sore throat 목 아픔 → since yesterday
- a runny nose 콧물 → since last night
- a cough 기침 → since Monday
- a headache 두통 → since this morning
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I*’ve had* a cold *since* Monday. 월요일부터 (지금까지) 감기예요.
*since* + 시작한 때 · *for* + 기간(two days)
물을 때: *How long have you had* it?
I have · I’ve got · I’ve had

I *have* a sore throat. = I*’ve got* a sore throat. (지금) 목이 아파요.
‘언제부터’를 붙이면: I*’ve had* it since yesterday.
errors: I have a sore throat since yesterday.
I’ve had a sore throat since yesterday.
I’ve had a cold since two days.
I’ve had a cold for two days.
two days 같은 기간 앞에는 for.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 현재완료 + since · for: I’ve had a cold since Monday. 월요일부터 (지금까지) 감기예요. / since + 시작한 때 · for + 기간(two days) / 물을 때: How long have you had it?
- I have · I’ve got · I’ve had: I have a sore throat. = I’ve got a sore throat. (지금) 목이 아파요. / ‘언제부터’를 붙이면: I’ve had it since yesterday.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I have a sore throat since yesterday. → I’ve had a sore throat since yesterday. (since(~부터 지금까지)와 함께면 I’ve had.)
- I’ve had a cold since two days. → I’ve had a cold for two days. (two days 같은 기간 앞에는 for.)
- Do I need prescription? → Do I need a prescription? (prescription 앞에 a를 넣어요.)
- It might makes you sleepy. → It might make you sleepy. (might 뒤에는 동사원형.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) a sore throat / yesterday → I’ve had a sore throat since yesterday. · 선생님이 약사 역할로 이어 물어요.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) a sore throat / yesterday → I’ve had a sore throat since yesterday. · 선생님이 약사 역할로 이어 물어요. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): a sore throat / yesterday | a runny nose / last night | a cough / Monday | a headache / this morning.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: How often should I take it?
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "I’ve had a sore throat since yesterday." (약국에서); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I don’t feel well." / "I’ve had a ___ since ___." / "How often should I take it?". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: How long have you had it?
If it gets worse, see a doctor.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 증상 말하기: "I have a sore throat." (목이 아파요., 보통); "I’ve got a runny nose." (콧물이 나요., 보통); "I can’t stop coughing." (기침이 멈추질 않아요., 보통)
- 약사에게 묻기: "Do I need a prescription?" (처방전이 필요해요?, 보통); "Are there any side effects?" (부작용이 있어요?, 보통)
- 약사가 하는 말: "How long have you had it?" (얼마나 됐어요?, 정중); "Take two tablets after meals." (식후에 두 알 드세요., 정중); "It might make you sleepy." (졸릴 수 있어요., 정중); "If it gets worse, see a doctor." (더 나빠지면 병원에 가 보세요., 정중); "I hope you feel better." (빨리 나으시길 바라요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

Picture words on screen. New: pharmacy (약국), pharmacist (약사), prescription (처방전), tablet (알약(납작한 정제)), pill (알약), painkiller (진통제), dose ((약의) 1회 복용량), sore throat (목 아픔, 인후통), runny nose (콧물(이 나는 코)), allergy (알레르기), blood pressure (혈압(blood 피)), first aid kit (구급상자).

After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "I work at the pharmacy counter. What are your symptoms? (역할 카드)" (hint on screen: I don’t feel well. I’ve had a sore throat since yesterday.)
- "How long have you had the runny nose? (역할 카드)" (hint on screen: For two days.)
- "Do you have any allergies? (역할 카드)" (hint on screen: No, I don’t. How often should I take it?)

Role card on screen (the learner may answer as this role): 건강은 역할 카드로만(실제 정보 ×): 여행 중인 손님 — 어제부터 목 아픔, 이틀째 콧물, 알레르기 없음. 양식의 Age / Sex도 가상으로.
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: A Quiet Afternoon
steps.text: The pharmacy was like a small supermarket, with vitamins for strong bones, cream for dry skin, and first aid cream to stop infection in small wounds. The actual pharmacy counter was at the back, and people *lined up* there with medical questions. After lunch, Jiwoo took the medicine and slept. *They say* honey helps a sore throat, so Daniel brought her honey and hot tea. By evening, the pain was gone, *more or less*. “A fast recovery!” said Daniel. “Just in time for movie night tomorrow!”

steps.title: 그 영화 봤어요?
steps.goal: 영화·드라마 내용을 말하고 평가하기
steps.scene_desc: 5월 초 밤, 시카고 대니얼 부모님 집 거실. 소파에 앉은 지우와 클로이가 리모컨을 들고 TV 속 영화 목록을 고르고, 뒤쪽 부엌에서 대니얼이 팝콘을 그릇에 담음(화면·포스터에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "What’s it about?" (그 영화 봤어요?). Goal: 영화·드라마 내용을 말하고 평가하기. Today's scene: 5월 초 밤, 시카고 대니얼 부모님 집 거실. 소파에 앉은 지우와 클로이가 리모컨을 들고 TV 속 영화 목록을 고르고, 뒤쪽 부엌에서 대니얼이 팝콘을 그릇에 담음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Chloe, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "It’s about ___.".

steps.when: 영화·드라마·책이 무슨 내용인지 짧게 말할 때 써요. about 뒤에 명사.

Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).

steps.title: Movie Night · 시카고 마지막 밤, 대니얼 부모님 집에서

lines.en: Okay, movie night! {{Have you seen}} “The Long Way Out”?
lines.ko: 자, 영화의 밤! ‘더 롱 웨이 아웃’ 봤어요?

lines.en: No, I haven’t. What’s it about?
lines.ko: 아뇨, 안 봤어요. 무슨 내용이에요?

lines.ko: 오, 범죄 영화네요! 실화예요?

lines.ko: 총이 많이 나와요? 무서운 영화는 싫거든요.

lines.en: Not many. The cast is great, and it won a lot of awards.
lines.ko: 별로요. 출연진도 좋고 상도 많이 받았어요.

lines.en: Or how about that romantic comedy? Or the musical?
lines.ko: 아니면 저 로맨틱 코미디는요? 뮤지컬은요?

lines.en: Hmm, that’s not really my thing. Trust me. It’s worth watching.
lines.ko: 음, 그건 제 취향이 아니에요. 믿어 봐요. 볼 만해요.

lines.en: (Later) Wow. The ending was so sad. The actors were great.
lines.ko: (영화가 끝나고) 와. 결말이 너무 슬펐어요. 배우들이 정말 좋았어요.

lines.en: That sounded so natural! So, what would you give it out of ten?
lines.ko: 정말 자연스러웠어요! 그래서 10점 만점에 몇 점 줄래요?

lines.en: {{I’d give it}} nine {{out of ten}}.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: It’s about ___. / It’s based on ___. / I’d give it ___ out of ten. / It’s worth watching. Table (장르 → 무슨 내용 (about)):
- a crime movie 범죄 영화 → It’s about a prisoner.
- a drama series 드라마 → It’s about three sisters.
- a musical 뮤지컬 → It’s about a young dancer.
- a comedy 코미디 → It’s about two neighbors.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
It’s *about* a prisoner. 죄수 이야기예요.
It’s *based on* a novel. 소설이 원작이에요.
물을 때: What’s it about? · Is it based on a book?

I’d give it *eight out of ten*. 10점 만점에 8점.
It’s worth *watching*. 볼 만해요.
I couldn’t stop *watching*. 멈출 수가 없었어요.

I don’t want to spoil it.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- about + 명사 · based on + 명사: It’s about a prisoner. 죄수 이야기예요. / It’s based on a novel. 소설이 원작이에요. / 물을 때: What’s it about? · Is it based on a book?
- 평가하는 말 · worth + -ing: I’d give it eight out of ten. 10점 만점에 8점. / It’s worth watching. 볼 만해요. / I couldn’t stop watching. 멈출 수가 없었어요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- It’s base on a novel. → It’s based on a novel. (‘~이 원작이에요’는 based on.)
- It’s worth to watch. → It’s worth watching. (worth 뒤에는 -ing.)
- I don’t want to spoiler it. → I don’t want to spoil it. (동사는 spoil. spoiler는 ‘스포일러’(명사).)
- The actors was great. → The actors were great. (actors(여럿) 뒤에는 were.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: about + 명사 · based on + 명사: It’s about a prisoner. 죄수 이야기예요.It’s based on a novel. 소설이 원작이에요.물을 때: What’s it about? · Is it based on a book?
평가하는 말 · worth + -ing: I’d give it eight out of ten. 10점 만점에 8점.It’s worth watching. 볼 만해요.I couldn’t stop watching. 멈출 수가 없었어요.
mistakes: It’s base on a novel. → It’s based on a novel.
It’s worth to watch. → It’s worth watching.
I don’t want to spoiler it. → I don’t want to spoil it.
The actors was great. → The actors were great.

steps.note: 예) a prisoner / a classic novel → It’s about a prisoner. It’s based on a classic novel. · 선생님이 What would you give it out of ten? 하고 이어 물어요.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) a prisoner / a classic novel → It’s about a prisoner. It’s based on a classic novel. · 선생님이 What would you give it out of ten? 하고 이어 물어요. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): a prisoner / a classic novel | three sisters / a web comic | a young dancer / a true story | a small town / a famous book.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: I’d give it ___ out of ten.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "What’s it about?" (그 영화 봤어요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "It’s about ___." / "It’s based on ___." / "I’d give it ___ out of ten.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I don’t want to spoil it.
It was a bit slow at first.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 묻고 내용 말하기: "Have you seen ___?" (~ 봤어요?, 보통); "What’s it about?" (무슨 내용이에요?, 보통); "It’s a true story." (실화예요., 보통); "I don’t want to spoil it." (스포하고 싶지 않아요., 친근)
- 본 느낌 말하기: "The ending was so sad." (결말이 너무 슬펐어요., 보통); "The actors were great." (배우들이 정말 좋았어요., 보통); "It was a bit slow at first." (처음엔 좀 느렸어요., 보통); "I couldn’t stop watching." (멈출 수가 없었어요., 친근)
- 권하기·취향 말하기: "It’s worth watching." (볼 만해요., 보통); "It’s not really my thing." (제 취향은 아니에요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 영화·드라마 장르

a *crime* movie 범죄 영화 · a *comedy* 코미디 · a *romantic* comedy 로맨틱 코미디
a *musical* 뮤지컬 · a *classic* 고전, 명작 · a scary movie 무서운 영화
스포 없이 말하기

No spoilers, please! 스포 금지요!

steps.blank:
A: Have you ___ “The Long Way Out”?   B: Yes! It’s ___ a prisoner. It’s ___ on a classic novel.
A: Is it good?   B: I’d give it nine ___ of ten. It’s worth ___.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 영화·드라마 장르: a crime movie 범죄 영화 · a comedy 코미디 · a romantic comedy 로맨틱 코미디 / a musical 뮤지컬 · a classic 고전, 명작 · a scary movie 무서운 영화
- 스포 없이 말하기: I don’t want to spoil it. 스포하고 싶지 않아요. / No spoilers, please! 스포 금지요! / the cast 출연진 · the plot 줄거리 · the ending 결말
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Have you ___ “The Long Way Out”? B: Yes! It’s ___ a prisoner. It’s ___ on a classic novel. / A: Is it good? B: I’d give it nine ___ of ten. It’s worth ___. / 낱말 상자: seen · about · based · out · watching
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

items.ko: 여자 배우(요즘은 actor로 다 부르기도 해요)

steps.teach:
Picture words on screen. New: film (영화), drama (드라마), series ((드라마) 시리즈), episode ((드라마의) 한 회, 1화), actor (배우), actress (여자 배우(요즘은 actor로 다 부르기도 해요)), director (감독), scene (장면), novel (소설), writer (작가), chapter ((책의) 장), character (등장인물).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: The film was released last year.
What’s the title of the movie?
Can you recommend a good drama?
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: movie (영화) — "Have you seen this movie?"; plot (줄거리) — "The plot is exciting."; based ((on과 함께) ~을 바탕으로 한) — "It’s based on a novel."; spoil ((내용을 미리 말해) 김새게 하다, 스포하다) — "Don’t spoil the ending!"; release (개봉하다, 공개하다) — "The film was released last year."; title (제목) — "What’s the title of the movie?"; ending (결말) — "The ending was so sad."; true (사실인, 실제의) — "It’s a true story."; recommend (추천하다) — "Can you recommend a good drama?".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Have you seen a good movie or drama lately?
What’s it about? Is it based on a book?
What would you give it out of ten?
I’d give it ___ out of ten.
What kind of movies are not really your thing?
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Have you seen a good movie or drama lately?" (hint on screen: Yes, I’ve seen ___. / Not really.)
- "What’s it about? Is it based on a book?" (hint on screen: It’s about ___. It’s based on ___.)
- "What would you give it out of ten?" (hint on screen: I’d give it ___ out of ten.)
- "What kind of movies are not really your thing?" (hint on screen: ___ are not really my thing.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: Have you seen a good movie or drama lately?
What’s it about? Is it based on a book?
What would you give it out of ten?
What kind of movies are not really your thing?

steps.title: Movie Night
steps.text: “Everyone gets an equal vote,” said Daniel’s mom. Four of the five votes went to “The Long Way Out.” His mom is a big reader, and she read the novel years ago. In the film, an evil prison boss hates the hero. During a storm, the lights *go off*, and there’s a mass escape. Later, everyone thinks the hero is dead, but… no spoilers! The story *slows down* in the middle, but nobody left the sofa. *Whether or not* you like crime films, the last scene is worth it. Jiwoo cried a little. “What a perfect last night in Chicago,” she said.
steps.gloss: equal 똑같은, 동등한 · vote 표, 투표 · reader 책 읽는 사람, 독자 · evil 사악한 · go off (불이) 꺼지다 · mass 대규모의, 한꺼번에 · dead 죽은 · slow down 느려지다 · whether or not ~이든 아니든 · shoot(shot) 촬영하다 · 작품명은 수업용 가상의 제목
questions: Who read the novel years ago?
What happens during the storm?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Movie Night". Text: "“Everyone gets an equal vote,” said Daniel’s mom. Four of the five votes went to “The Long Way Out.” His mom is a big reader, and she read the novel years ago. In the film, an evil prison boss hates the hero. During a storm, the lights go off, and there’s a mass escape. Later, everyone thinks the hero is dead, but… no spoilers! The story slows down in the middle, but nobody left the sofa. Whether or not you like crime films, the last scene is worth it. Jiwoo cried a little. “What a perfect last night in Chicago,” she said." Words: equal 똑같은, 동등한 · vote 표, 투표 · reader 책 읽는 사람, 독자 · evil 사악한 · go off (불이) 꺼지다 · mass 대규모의, 한꺼번에 · dead 죽은 · slow down 느려지다 · whether or not ~이든 아니든 · shoot(shot) 촬영하다 · 작품명은 수업용 가상의 제목.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Who read the novel years ago?" / "What happens during the storm?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘It’s about ___.’로 영화·드라마 내용을 짧게 말할 수 있어요.
‘It’s based on ___.’로 원작이나 실화를 말할 수 있어요.
‘I’d give it ___ out of ten.’으로 점수를 매겨 평가할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘It’s about ___.’로 영화·드라마 내용을 짧게 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘It’s based on ___.’로 원작이나 실화를 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘I’d give it ___ out of ten.’으로 점수를 매겨 평가할 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

lessons.title: 무슨 일이 있었냐면
lessons.goal: 있었던 일을 꺼내고, 순서대로 말하고, 결말을 말하기

steps.title: 무슨 일이 있었냐면
steps.goal: 있었던 일을 꺼내고, 순서대로 말하고, 결말을 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 6월 초 토요일 오전, 서울 아파트 건물 앞 벤치. 장바구니를 든 벤이 눈을 크게 뜨고 듣고, 지우가 두 손으로 기차가 떠나는 시늉을 하며 이야기함(간판·글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "You won’t believe what happened!" (무슨 일이 있었냐면). Goal: 있었던 일을 꺼내고, 순서대로 말하고, 결말을 말하기. Today's scene: 6월 초 토요일 오전, 서울 아파트 건물 앞 벤치. 장바구니를 든 벤이 눈을 크게 뜨고 듣고, 지우가 두 손으로 기차가 떠나는 시늉을 하며 이야기함. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Ben, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "You won’t believe what happened!".

steps.ko: 무슨 일이 있었는지 들으면 못 믿을걸요!
steps.when: 놀라운 이야기를 꺼낼 때 써요. 듣는 사람이 궁금해지게 해요.
steps.extra: 대답: What happened? · Tell me!
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "You won’t believe what happened!" (무슨 일이 있었는지 들으면 못 믿을걸요!). When to use it: 놀라운 이야기를 꺼낼 때 써요. 듣는 사람이 궁금해지게 해요. Note: 대답: What happened? · Tell me!
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "First, ___. Then ___.".

steps.when: 일어난 일을 순서대로 말해요. 지난 일이라 과거형으로 이어요.
steps.extra: First, I went to the restroom. Then I missed my train.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "First, ___. Then ___." (먼저 ~. 그다음에 ~.). When to use it: 일어난 일을 순서대로 말해요. 지난 일이라 과거형으로 이어요. Note: First, I went to the restroom. Then I missed my train.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "In the end, ___.".

steps.when: 이런저런 일 끝에 어떻게 됐는지, 이야기의 결말을 말해요.
steps.extra: In the end, it turned out fine.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "In the end, ___." (결국 ~.). When to use it: 이런저런 일 끝에 어떻게 됐는지, 이야기의 결말을 말해요. Note: In the end, it turned out fine.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Back Home · 6월 초 토요일, 아파트 앞에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Back Home · 6월 초 토요일, 아파트 앞에서

lines.en: Jiwoo! Welcome back! How was the trip?
lines.ko: 지우! 잘 다녀왔어요! 여행 어땠어요?

lines.en: Amazing! But {{you won’t believe what happened}}. I missed my train to Chicago!
lines.ko: 정말 좋았어요! 그런데 무슨 일이 있었는지 들으면 못 믿을걸요. 시카고 가는 기차를 놓쳤어요!

lines.en: No way! How did that happen?
lines.ko: 말도 안 돼! 어쩌다가요?

lines.en: {{First}}, I went to the restroom. {{Then}} I came back, and the train was gone!
lines.ko: 먼저 화장실에 갔어요. 그다음에 돌아왔는데 기차가 떠나 버렸어요!

lines.en: Oh no! What happened next?
lines.ko: 이런! 그다음엔 어떻게 됐어요?

lines.en: Luckily, a station worker helped me. After that, I took the next train.
lines.ko: 다행히 역 직원이 도와줬어요. 그 뒤에 다음 기차를 탔어요.

lines.en: So you got to Chicago, and that’s it?
lines.ko: 그래서 시카고에 도착했고, 그걸로 끝이에요?

lines.en: Not even close! Unfortunately, I got lost outside the station. A kind stranger came to my rescue.
lines.ko: 전혀요! 안타깝게도 역 밖에서 길을 잃었어요. 친절한 낯선 분이 저를 도와줬어요.

lines.en: Ha! So, how did it all end?
lines.ko: 하하! 그래서 결국 어떻게 됐어요?

lines.en: {{In the end}}, it turned out fine. It’s my favorite story now!
lines.ko: 결국 다 잘됐어요. 이젠 제일 좋아하는 이야기예요!

lines.en: Bad trips make the best stories. Wait till you hear mine!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Back Home · 6월 초 토요일, 아파트 앞에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Ben: "Jiwoo! Welcome back! How was the trip?" (지우! 잘 다녀왔어요! 여행 어땠어요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Amazing! But you won’t believe what happened. I missed my train to Chicago!" (정말 좋았어요! 그런데 무슨 일이 있었는지 들으면 못 믿을걸요. 시카고 가는 기차를 놓쳤어요!)
3. Ben: "No way! How did that happen?" (말도 안 돼! 어쩌다가요?)
4. Jiwoo: "First, I went to the restroom. Then I came back, and the train was gone!" (먼저 화장실에 갔어요. 그다음에 돌아왔는데 기차가 떠나 버렸어요!)
5. Ben: "Oh no! What happened next?" (이런! 그다음엔 어떻게 됐어요?)
6. Jiwoo: "Luckily, a station worker helped me. After that, I took the next train." (다행히 역 직원이 도와줬어요. 그 뒤에 다음 기차를 탔어요.)
7. Ben: "So you got to Chicago, and that’s it?" (그래서 시카고에 도착했고, 그걸로 끝이에요?)
8. Jiwoo: "Not even close! Unfortunately, I got lost outside the station. A kind stranger came to my rescue." (전혀요! 안타깝게도 역 밖에서 길을 잃었어요. 친절한 낯선 분이 저를 도와줬어요.)
9. Ben: "Ha! So, how did it all end?" (하하! 그래서 결국 어떻게 됐어요?)
10. Jiwoo: "In the end, it turned out fine. It’s my favorite story now!" (결국 다 잘됐어요. 이젠 제일 좋아하는 이야기예요!)
11. Ben: "Bad trips make the best stories. Wait till you hear mine!" (고생한 여행이 제일 좋은 이야깃거리죠. 내 얘기도 들어 봐요!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.
