steps.title: 조언하기
steps.goal: 조언을 구하고, If I were you로 조언하고, 조언에 답하기
steps.scene_desc: 12월 초 평일 저녁, 회사 근처 카페 창가 자리. 창밖은 어둡고 작은 전구 장식이 반짝임. 퇴근한 지우가 머그잔을 두 손으로 감싸고 고민스러운 얼굴로 이야기하고, 마야가 몸을 앞으로 기울여 들으며 고개를 끄덕임
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "What should I do?" (조언하기). Goal: 조언을 구하고, If I were you로 조언하고, 조언에 답하기. Today's scene: 12월 초 평일 저녁, 회사 근처 카페 창가 자리. 창밖은 어둡고 작은 전구 장식이 반짝임. 퇴근한 지우가 머그잔을 두 손으로 감싸고 고민스러운 얼굴로 이야기하고, 마야가 몸을 앞으로 기울여 들으며 고개를 끄덕임. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Maya, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "What should I do?".

steps.when: 고민을 먼저 말하고 조언을 구할 때 써요.
steps.extra: My job is so boring. What should I do?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "What should I do?" (어떻게 하면 좋을까요?). When to use it: 고민을 먼저 말하고 조언을 구할 때 써요. Note: My job is so boring. What should I do?
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "If I were you, I’d ___.".

steps.when: 상대 입장이 되어 조언할 때 써요. I’d(= I would) 뒤에는 *동사원형*.
steps.extra: If I were you, I’d talk to your team leader.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "If I were you, I’d ___." (내가 당신이라면 ~하겠어요.). When to use it: 상대 입장이 되어 조언할 때 써요. I’d(= I would) 뒤에는 동사원형. Note: If I were you, I’d talk to your team leader.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "That’s a good idea.".

steps.when: 조언이나 제안이 마음에 들 때 써요.
steps.extra: A: Why don’t you take a class? B: That’s a good idea.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "That’s a good idea." (좋은 생각이에요.). When to use it: 조언이나 제안이 마음에 들 때 써요. Note: A: Why don’t you take a class? B: That’s a good idea.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("A Little Advice · 12월 초 저녁, 회사 근처 카페에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: A Little Advice · 12월 초 저녁, 회사 근처 카페에서

lines.en: Jiwoo, you’re so quiet tonight. Is everything okay?
lines.ko: 지우 씨, 오늘 저녁 정말 조용하네요. 괜찮아요?

lines.en: To be honest, I’ve been struggling at work lately. Can I ask your advice?
lines.ko: 솔직히 요즘 회사 일로 좀 힘들어요. 조언 좀 구해도 될까요?

lines.en: Of course. What’s the situation?
lines.ko: 그럼요. 무슨 상황인데요?

lines.en: I make the same banners every day. It’s easy, but I’m bored. I want to try app design. {{What should I do?}}
lines.ko: 매일 똑같은 배너를 만들어요. 쉽긴 한데 지루해요. 앱 디자인을 해 보고 싶어요. 어떻게 하면 좋을까요?

lines.en: {{If I were you, I’d}} talk to your team leader. Ask for a different kind of project.
lines.ko: 내가 지우 씨라면 팀장님께 말해 보겠어요. 다른 종류의 프로젝트를 달라고 해 봐요.

lines.en: But what if my team leader refuses?
lines.ko: 그런데 팀장님이 거절하면요?

lines.en: Then find another solution. Have you tried taking an online course?
lines.ko: 그럼 다른 방법을 찾으면 돼요. 온라인 강좌를 들어 봤어요?

lines.en: Not yet. {{That’s a good idea.}} Honestly, I sometimes think about a new job, too.
lines.ko: 아직이요. 좋은 생각이에요. 솔직히 가끔은 새 직장도 생각해요.

lines.en: That’s a big decision. I wouldn’t hurry if I were you. Think about it carefully.
lines.ko: 그건 큰 결정이에요. 내가 지우 씨라면 서두르지 않겠어요. 신중하게 생각해 봐요.

lines.en: You’re right. Thanks, Maya. That really helps.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 고마워요, 마야. 정말 도움이 돼요.

lines.en: Anytime. You’ve got this!
lines.ko: 언제든지요. 잘할 거예요!

…I’d put down my phone at night.
Thanks, I’ll give it a try.
…I’d go for a walk after lunch.
I spend too much. 돈을 너무 써요
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: ___. What should I do? / If I were you, I’d ___. Table (고민 → 조언 (If I were you, I’d …)):
- My job is boring. 일이 지루해요 → …I’d ask for a new project.
- I can’t sleep well. 잠을 잘 못 자요 → …I’d put down my phone at night.
- I’m always tired. 늘 피곤해요 → …I’d go for a walk after lunch.
- I spend too much. 돈을 너무 써요 → …I’d write down what I buy.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: If I were you, I’d + 동사원형

상상이라서 *were*(was도 들리지만 were로 익혀요), 뒤에는 *I’d*(= I would) + 동사원형.
If I *were* you, *I’d talk* to her.
하지 말라고: I *wouldn’t* hurry if I were you.

You *should* ~. (분명하게) · If I were you, I’d ~.
*Why don’t you* ~? · *Have you tried* ~ing?
It *might* be a good idea *to* ~. (아주 부드럽게)
errors: If I were you, I will talk to her.
If I were you, I’d talk to her.
If I were you 뒤에는 I’d(= I would).
If I were you, I’d to talk to her.
If I were you, I’d talk to her.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- If I were you, I’d + 동사원형: 상상이라서 were(was도 들리지만 were로 익혀요), 뒤에는 I’d(= I would) + 동사원형. / If I were you, I’d talk to her. / 하지 말라고: I wouldn’t hurry if I were you.
- 조언하는 말 · 세기 차이: You should ~. (분명하게) · If I were you, I’d ~. / Why don’t you ~? · Have you tried ~ing? / It might be a good idea to ~. (아주 부드럽게)
Common mistakes on screen:
- If I were you, I will talk to her. → If I were you, I’d talk to her. (If I were you 뒤에는 I’d(= I would).)
- If I were you, I’d to talk to her. → If I were you, I’d talk to her. (I’d 뒤에는 to 없이 동사원형.)
- Can I ask your advices? → Can I ask your advice? (advice(조언)에는 -s를 붙이지 않아요.)
- Can you advice me? → Can you advise me? (‘조언하다’(동사)는 advise.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: If I were you, I’d + 동사원형: 상상이라서 were(was도 들리지만 were로 익혀요), 뒤에는 I’d(= I would) + 동사원형.If I were you, I’d talk to her.하지 말라고: I wouldn’t hurry if I were you.
조언하는 말 · 세기 차이: You should ~. (분명하게) · If I were you, I’d ~.Why don’t you ~? · Have you tried ~ing?It might be a good idea to ~. (아주 부드럽게)
mistakes: If I were you, I will talk to her. → If I were you, I’d talk to her.
If I were you, I’d to talk to her. → If I were you, I’d talk to her.
Can I ask your advices? → Can I ask your advice?
Can you advice me? → Can you advise me?

steps.note: 예) My job is boring. / ask for a new project → My job is boring. What should I do? — If I were you, I’d ask for a new project.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) My job is boring. / ask for a new project → My job is boring. What should I do? — If I were you, I’d ask for a new project. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): My job is boring. / ask for a new project | I’m always tired. / go to bed earlier | I can’t decide. / make a list | My room is a mess. / clean one corner a day.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "What should I do?" (조언하기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What should I do?" / "If I were you, I’d ___." / "That’s a good idea.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: It might be a good idea to ___.
I wouldn’t ___ if I were you.
Thanks, I’ll give it a try.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 조언 구하기: "Can I ask your advice?" (조언 좀 구해도 될까요?, 보통); "What would you do?" (당신이라면 어떻게 하겠어요?, 보통)
- 조언하기: "Why don’t you ___?" (~하면 어때요?, 친근); "Have you tried ___ing?" (~해 봤어요?, 보통); "It might be a good idea to ___." (~하는 것도 좋을 거예요., 정중); "I wouldn’t ___ if I were you." (내가 당신이라면 ~하지 않겠어요., 보통)
- 조언에 답하기: "Thanks, I’ll give it a try." (고마워요, 한번 해 볼게요., 보통); "That really helps." (정말 도움이 돼요., 보통); "I’ll think about it." (생각해 볼게요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: advice · advise

Can I ask your *advice*? 조언(명사) — -s 없이, 하나는 a piece of advice
What would you *advise*? 조언하다(동사)
소리도 달라요: advi*c*e [s] · advi*s*e [z]
put down · care for

*put down* your phone 휴대폰을 내려놓다 · *put down* your goals 목표를 적어 두다
I don’t really *care for* it. 그건 별로 안 좋아해요.
Grace *cares for* her plants. 그레이스는 화분을 돌봐요.
steps.blank:
A: My job is so boring. What ___ I do?   B: If I ___ you, I’d talk to your team leader.
A: That’s a good ___. Thanks!   B: And have you ___ taking an online course?
낱말 상자: should · were · idea · tried
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- advice · advise: Can I ask your advice? 조언(명사) — -s 없이, 하나는 a piece of advice / What would you advise? 조언하다(동사) / 소리도 달라요: advice [s] · advise [z]
- put down · care for: put down your phone 휴대폰을 내려놓다 · put down your goals 목표를 적어 두다 / I don’t really care for it. 그건 별로 안 좋아해요. / Grace cares for her plants. 그레이스는 화분을 돌봐요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: My job is so boring. What ___ I do? B: If I ___ you, I’d talk to your team leader. / A: That’s a good ___. Thanks! B: And have you ___ taking an online course? / 낱말 상자: should · were · idea · tried
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: advice (조언), problem (문제), help (돕다; 도움), struggle (애쓰다, 힘들어하다), refuse (거절하다), careful (조심하는, 신중한), handle ((일을) 처리하다, 다루다), solution (해결책), try (해 보다, 시도하다). Review words: idea (생각, 아이디어), decision (결정), option (선택지, 고를 수 있는 것).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: It might be a good idea.
Talking early can prevent bigger problems.
I had difficulty sleeping last night.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: advise (조언하다) — "What would you advise?"; should (~하는 게 좋다) — "You should get some rest."; might (~할지도 모른다) — "It might be a good idea."; situation (상황) — "What’s the situation?"; prevent (막다, 예방하다) — "Talking early can prevent bigger problems."; carefully (신중하게, 조심해서) — "Think about it carefully."; difficulty (어려움) — "I had difficulty sleeping last night."; suggest (제안하다) — "Can I suggest something?"; honest (솔직한) — "To be honest, I’m bored."; worth (~할 가치가 있는) — "It’s worth a try.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: I’m always tired after work. What should I do?
I want to improve my English. Can I ask your advice?
Have you tried ___ing? / Why don’t you ___?
What’s the best advice you’ve ever heard?
Do you like giving advice? Why or why not?
Think of a small everyday problem and ask me for advice.
Can I ask your advice? ___. What should I do? (예: 방 정리, 취미 고르기, 영어 연습 시간)
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "I’m always tired after work. What should I do?" (hint on screen: If I were you, I’d ___.)
- "I want to improve my English. Can I ask your advice?" (hint on screen: Have you tried ___ing? / Why don’t you ___?)
- "What’s the best advice you’ve ever heard?" (hint on screen: The best advice was “___.”)
- "Do you like giving advice? Why or why not?" (hint on screen: Yes, because ___. / Not really. I ___.)
- "Think of a small everyday problem and ask me for advice." (hint on screen: Can I ask your advice? ___. What should I do? (예: 방 정리, 취미 고르기, 영어 연습 시간))
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: I’m always tired after work. What should I do?
I want to improve my English. Can I ask your advice?
What’s the best advice you’ve ever heard?
Do you like giving advice? Why or why not?
Think of a small everyday problem and ask me for advice.

steps.title: Two Lists
steps.text: That night, Jiwoo thought carefully about Maya’s advice. In a notebook, she *put down* two lists. The first was things she loves: drawing, solving problems, and working with people. The second was things she doesn’t really *care for*: the same banners every day and last-minute changes. On paper, her situation looked clearer. She still loves design. She just wants a new challenge. First, she’ll ask her team leader for a new kind of project. Then she’ll look for an online course. A new job? Maybe someday, but not yet. She texted Maya, “No big decisions. Just small steps.”
steps.gloss: put down 적어 두다(‘내려놓다’라는 뜻도 있어요) · not care for 별로 안 좋아하다 · last-minute 막판의 · clearer 더 분명한 · challenge 도전 · text 문자를 보내다
questions: What did Jiwoo put down in her notebook?
What is Jiwoo going to ask her team leader for?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Two Lists". Text: "That night, Jiwoo thought carefully about Maya’s advice. In a notebook, she put down two lists. The first was things she loves: drawing, solving problems, and working with people. The second was things she doesn’t really care for: the same banners every day and last-minute changes. On paper, her situation looked clearer. She still loves design. She just wants a new challenge. First, she’ll ask her team leader for a new kind of project. Then she’ll look for an online course. A new job? Maybe someday, but not yet. She texted Maya, “No big decisions. Just small steps.”" Words: put down 적어 두다(‘내려놓다’라는 뜻도 있어요) · not care for 별로 안 좋아하다 · last-minute 막판의 · clearer 더 분명한 · challenge 도전 · text 문자를 보내다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Jiwoo put down in her notebook?" / "What is Jiwoo going to ask her team leader for?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘What should I do?’로 고민을 말하고 조언을 구할 수 있어요.
‘If I were you, I’d ___.’로 상대 입장에서 조언할 수 있어요.
‘That’s a good idea. / I’ll think about it.’으로 조언에 답할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘What should I do?’로 고민을 말하고 조언을 구할 수 있어요.
- ‘If I were you, I’d ___.’로 상대 입장에서 조언할 수 있어요.
- ‘That’s a good idea. / I’ll think about it.’으로 조언에 답할 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

lessons.title: 새해 계획
lessons.title_en: I’m thinking of taking a course.
lessons.goal: 계획을 묻고, 생각 중인 계획을 말하고, 응원하기

steps.title: 새해 계획
steps.title_en: I’m thinking of taking a course.
steps.goal: 계획을 묻고, 생각 중인 계획을 말하고, 응원하기
steps.scene_desc: 12월 중순 저녁, 그레이스네 아늑한 거실. 탁자 위에 찻잔 두 개, 귤 한 접시, 펼친 공책과 펜. 그레이스가 펜을 들고 웃으며 묻고, 지우가 손가락을 꼽으며 대답함
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "I’m thinking of taking a course." (새해 계획). Goal: 계획을 묻고, 생각 중인 계획을 말하고, 응원하기. Today's scene: 12월 중순 저녁, 그레이스네 아늑한 거실. 탁자 위에 찻잔 두 개, 귤 한 접시, 펼친 공책과 펜. 그레이스가 펜을 들고 웃으며 묻고, 지우가 손가락을 꼽으며 대답함. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Grace, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Do you have any plans for ___?".

steps.en: Do you have any plans for ___?
steps.when: 다가오는 때의 계획을 물을 때 써요. for 뒤에 때를 넣어요.
steps.extra: Do you have any plans for next year? · Do you have any plans for the weekend?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Do you have any plans for ___?" (~에 무슨 계획 있어요?). When to use it: 다가오는 때의 계획을 물을 때 써요. for 뒤에 때를 넣어요. Note: Do you have any plans for next year? · Do you have any plans for the weekend?
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I’m thinking of ___ing.".

steps.when: 아직 확실히 정하지 않은 계획을 말해요. of 뒤에는 *동사 + ing*.
steps.extra: I’m thinking of taking an online course.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I’m thinking of ___ing." (~할까 생각 중이에요.). When to use it: 아직 확실히 정하지 않은 계획을 말해요. of 뒤에는 동사 + ing. Note: I’m thinking of taking an online course.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I hope it works out!".

steps.when: 상대의 계획을 응원할 때 써요. work out은 ‘잘 풀리다’.
steps.extra: 대답: Thanks! I’ll let you know.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I hope it works out!" (잘되길 바라요!). When to use it: 상대의 계획을 응원할 때 써요. work out은 ‘잘 풀리다’. Note: 대답: Thanks! I’ll let you know.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: Do you have any plans for ___? / I’m thinking of ___ing. Table (때 (Do you have any plans for …?) → 생각 중인 계획 (I’m thinking of …)):
- next year 내년 → …taking a course.
- this winter 이번 겨울 → …learning to ski.
- the holidays 연휴 → …reading more books.
- the weekend 주말 → …trying a new café.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
아직 확실히 정하지 않은 계획이에요. of 뒤에는 동사에 *-ing*.
I’m thinking of *taking* a course.
물을 때: Are you thinking of *quitting*?

I’m thinking of ~ing. 생각 중
I’m planning to ~. 계획 중 · I’m going to ~. 하기로 함
아직이면: I haven’t decided yet.
errors: I’m thinking of take a course.
I’m thinking of taking a course.
My goal is to save money.
‘~하는 것’이 목표면 is 뒤에 to + 동사원형.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- I’m thinking of + 동사 ~ing: 아직 확실히 정하지 않은 계획이에요. of 뒤에는 동사에 -ing. / I’m thinking of taking a course. / 물을 때: Are you thinking of quitting?
- 얼마나 정했나: I’m thinking of ~ing. 생각 중 / I’m planning to ~. 계획 중 · I’m going to ~. 하기로 함 / 아직이면: I haven’t decided yet.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’m thinking of take a course. → I’m thinking of taking a course. (of 뒤에는 ~ing.)
- My goal is save money. → My goal is to save money. (‘~하는 것’이 목표면 is 뒤에 to + 동사원형.)
- I hope it work out! → I hope it works out! (it 뒤라서 works.)
- I haven’t decide yet. → I haven’t decided yet. (haven’t 뒤에는 p.p.(decided).)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) next year / taking an online course → Do you have any plans for next year? — I’m thinking of taking an online course.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) next year / taking an online course → Do you have any plans for next year? — I’m thinking of taking an online course. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): next year / taking an online course | this winter / learning to ski | the holidays / reading more books | next month / joining a gym.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "I’m thinking of taking a course." (새해 계획); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Do you have any plans for ___?" / "I’m thinking of ___ing." / "I hope it works out!". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 계획 말하기: "My goal is to ___." (제 목표는 ~하는 거예요., 보통); "I’m planning to ___." (~할 계획이에요., 보통); "This year, I want to ___." (올해는 ~하고 싶어요., 보통); "I haven’t decided yet." (아직 안 정했어요., 보통)

Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Grace’s Annual Goals
steps.text: Every December, Grace writes her annual goals in a small notebook. She has done it for almost a decade. As an English teacher, she calls them her ‘objectives.’ First, she’s thinking of launching a book club at the library. Second, she wants to run a 10K race in the fall. Jiwoo showed Grace her list, too: an online course, more exercise, and saving money every month. Grace smiled. “*No doubt* you’ll succeed. And when things get hard, *reach out* to a friend.” They agreed to check their lists again in June.

questions: What does Grace write every December?
What’s on Jiwoo’s list?

steps.title: 습관 바꾸기
steps.goal: 그만둔 습관과 새로 시작한 습관 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 12월 중순 이른 아침, 아파트 지하 주민 운동실. 운동복 차림의 지우가 매트 위에서 스트레칭을 하고, 옆에서 벤이 실내 자전거를 타며 웃으며 이야기함(벽·기계 화면에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Old habits die hard." (습관 바꾸기). Goal: 그만둔 습관과 새로 시작한 습관 말하기. Today's scene: 12월 중순 이른 아침, 아파트 지하 주민 운동실. 운동복 차림의 지우가 매트 위에서 스트레칭을 하고, 옆에서 벤이 실내 자전거를 타며 웃으며 이야기함. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Ben, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I’m trying to ___.".

steps.when: 요즘 바꾸려고 애쓰는 습관을 말할 때 써요. trying to 뒤에는 동사원형.
steps.extra: I’m trying to sleep more. · I’m trying to eat healthier.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I’m trying to ___." (~하려고 노력 중이에요.). When to use it: 요즘 바꾸려고 애쓰는 습관을 말할 때 써요. trying to 뒤에는 동사원형. Note: I’m trying to sleep more. · I’m trying to eat healthier.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I gave up ___ing.".

steps.when: 오래 하던 일을 끊었다고 말해요. give up의 과거형은 *gave up*, 뒤에는 *-ing*.
steps.extra: I gave up drinking coffee after lunch.

(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).

steps.title: Morning Routine · 12월 중순 아침, 아파트 운동실에서

lines.en: Morning, Jiwoo! Still exercising every morning? Good for you!
lines.ko: 좋은 아침, 지우 씨! 아직도 매일 아침 운동하네요? 대단해요!

lines.en: Thanks! But I’m always tired. I used to look at my phone screen in bed for hours.
lines.ko: 고마워요! 그런데 늘 피곤해요. 예전엔 침대에서 몇 시간씩 휴대폰 화면을 봤거든요.

lines.en: Ah, I know that habit. So what did you change?
lines.ko: 아, 그 습관 알죠. 그래서 뭘 바꿨어요?

lines.en: {{I’m trying to}} sort out my sleep. {{I’ve started}} leaving my phone in the kitchen. When my alarm goes off, I have to get up!
lines.ko: 잠을 바로잡으려고 노력 중이에요. 휴대폰을 부엌에 두기 시작했어요. 알람이 울리면 일어나야 하죠!

lines.en: Ha! Smart. Is it working?
lines.ko: 하! 똑똑하네요. 효과 있어요?

lines.en: Yes, but it’s harder than I thought. I keep forgetting. Old habits… don’t die easily?
lines.ko: 네, 그런데 생각보다 어려워요. 자꾸 잊어버려요. 오랜 습관은… 쉽게 안 죽는다?

lines.en: Close! Here’s how people really say it: “Old habits die hard.”
lines.ko: 거의 맞았어요! 원어민은 실제로 이렇게 말해요. “오랜 습관은 잘 안 고쳐진다.”

lines.en: Old habits die hard. What about you, Ben?
lines.ko: 오랜 습관은 잘 안 고쳐진다. 벤은요?

lines.en: {{I gave up}} drinking coffee after lunch. I used to have four cups a day!
lines.ko: 점심 이후엔 커피를 끊었어요. 예전엔 하루에 네 잔 마셨거든요!

lines.en: Four cups? How did you do it?
lines.ko: 네 잔이요? 어떻게 했어요?

lines.en: Little by little. Now I drink tea in the afternoon, and I sleep much better.
lines.ko: 조금씩요. 이제 오후엔 차를 마시고, 잠도 훨씬 잘 자요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Morning Routine · 12월 중순 아침, 아파트 운동실에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Ben: "Morning, Jiwoo! Still exercising every morning? Good for you!" (좋은 아침, 지우 씨! 아직도 매일 아침 운동하네요? 대단해요!)

3. Ben: "Ah, I know that habit. So what did you change?" (아, 그 습관 알죠. 그래서 뭘 바꿨어요?)
4. Jiwoo: "I’m trying to sort out my sleep. I’ve started leaving my phone in the kitchen. When my alarm goes off, I have to get up!" (잠을 바로잡으려고 노력 중이에요. 휴대폰을 부엌에 두기 시작했어요. 알람이 울리면 일어나야 하죠!)
5. Ben: "Ha! Smart. Is it working?" (하! 똑똑하네요. 효과 있어요?)
6. Jiwoo: "Yes, but it’s harder than I thought. I keep forgetting. Old habits… don’t die easily?" (네, 그런데 생각보다 어려워요. 자꾸 잊어버려요. 오랜 습관은… 쉽게 안 죽는다?)
7. Ben: "Close! Here’s how people really say it: “Old habits die hard.”" (거의 맞았어요! 원어민은 실제로 이렇게 말해요. “오랜 습관은 잘 안 고쳐진다.”)
8. Jiwoo: "Old habits die hard. What about you, Ben?" (오랜 습관은 잘 안 고쳐진다. 벤은요?)
9. Ben: "I gave up drinking coffee after lunch. I used to have four cups a day!" (점심 이후엔 커피를 끊었어요. 예전엔 하루에 네 잔 마셨거든요!)
10. Jiwoo: "Four cups? How did you do it?" (네 잔이요? 어떻게 했어요?)
11. Ben: "Little by little. Now I drink tea in the afternoon, and I sleep much better." (조금씩요. 이제 오후엔 차를 마시고, 잠도 훨씬 잘 자요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

steps.teach:
Role reading of the same scene. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Ben exactly as written, word for word. Never change, add or skip a line, and never read the learner's lines for them first.
1. Ben (you): "Morning, Jiwoo! Still exercising every morning? Good for you!" (좋은 아침, 지우 씨! 아직도 매일 아침 운동하네요? 대단해요!)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "Thanks! But I’m always tired. I used to look at my phone screen in bed for hours." (고마워요! 그런데 늘 피곤해요. 예전엔 침대에서 몇 시간씩 휴대폰 화면을 봤거든요.)
3. Ben (you): "Ah, I know that habit. So what did you change?" (아, 그 습관 알죠. 그래서 뭘 바꿨어요?)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "I’m trying to sort out my sleep. I’ve started leaving my phone in the kitchen. When my alarm goes off, I have to get up!" (잠을 바로잡으려고 노력 중이에요. 휴대폰을 부엌에 두기 시작했어요. 알람이 울리면 일어나야 하죠!)
5. Ben (you): "Ha! Smart. Is it working?" (하! 똑똑하네요. 효과 있어요?)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "Yes, but it’s harder than I thought. I keep forgetting. Old habits… don’t die easily?" (네, 그런데 생각보다 어려워요. 자꾸 잊어버려요. 오랜 습관은… 쉽게 안 죽는다?)
7. Ben (you): "Close! Here’s how people really say it: “Old habits die hard.”" (거의 맞았어요! 원어민은 실제로 이렇게 말해요. “오랜 습관은 잘 안 고쳐진다.”)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "Old habits die hard. What about you, Ben?" (오랜 습관은 잘 안 고쳐진다. 벤은요?)
9. Ben (you): "I gave up drinking coffee after lunch. I used to have four cups a day!" (점심 이후엔 커피를 끊었어요. 예전엔 하루에 네 잔 마셨거든요!)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "Four cups? How did you do it?" (네 잔이요? 어떻게 했어요?)
11. Ben (you): "Little by little. Now I drink tea in the afternoon, and I sleep much better." (조금씩요. 이제 오후엔 차를 마시고, 잠도 훨씬 잘 자요.)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Ben. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: Jiwoo used to look at her phone in bed for hours.
Jiwoo keeps her phone next to her bed now.

1. Jiwoo used to look at her phone in bed for hours. → True (line 2)
2. Jiwoo keeps her phone next to her bed now. → False (line 4)
3. Ben drinks coffee in the afternoon. → False (line 9, 11)

Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: Are you trying to change any habits? / How did you do it?
I’m trying to ___. / I gave up ___ing. / I’ve started ___ing.
head: 그만둔 것 (gave up + -ing)
새로 시작한 것 (have started + -ing)
rows: I *gave up* eating late at night.
I *gave up* checking my phone in bed.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: Are you trying to change any habits? / How did you do it? / I’m trying to ___. / I gave up ___ing. / I’ve started ___ing. Table (그만둔 것 (gave up + -ing) → 새로 시작한 것 (have started + -ing)):
- I gave up eating late at night. → I’ve started going to bed earlier.
- I gave up eating sweets. → I’ve started drinking more water.
- I gave up taking the elevator. → I’ve started walking up the stairs.
- I gave up checking my phone in bed. → I’ve started reading before bed.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
그만둔 일: I *gave up* drinking coffee. = I *quit* drinking coffee.
give up·quit 뒤에 오는 동사는 *-ing*: give up drink*ing*

I’m *trying to* eat healthier. 요즘 애쓰는 중(to + 동사원형)
I’ve *started* going to bed earlier. 최근에 시작해서 지금도 해요.
errors: I’ve start going to bed earlier.
I’ve started going to bed earlier.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- give up · quit + -ing: 그만둔 일: I gave up drinking coffee. = I quit drinking coffee. / give up·quit 뒤에 오는 동사는 -ing: give up drinking
- trying to · have started: I’m trying to eat healthier. 요즘 애쓰는 중(to + 동사원형) / I’ve started going to bed earlier. 최근에 시작해서 지금도 해요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I gave up drink coffee. → I gave up drinking coffee. (give up 뒤에는 -ing.)
- I’m trying eat healthier. → I’m trying to eat healthier. (애쓰는 일은 trying to + 동사원형.)
- I keep forget. → I keep forgetting. (‘자꾸 ~해요’는 keep + -ing.)
- I’ve start going to bed earlier. → I’ve started going to bed earlier. (I’ve(I have) 뒤에는 started.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: give up · quit + -ing: 그만둔 일: I gave up drinking coffee. = I quit drinking coffee.give up·quit 뒤에 오는 동사는 -ing: give up drinking
trying to · have started: I’m trying to eat healthier. 요즘 애쓰는 중(to + 동사원형)I’ve started going to bed earlier. 최근에 시작해서 지금도 해요.
mistakes: I gave up drink coffee. → I gave up drinking coffee.
I’m trying eat healthier. → I’m trying to eat healthier.
I keep forget. → I keep forgetting.
I’ve start going to bed earlier. → I’ve started going to bed earlier.

steps.note: 예) drinking coffee / drinking tea → I gave up drinking coffee. I’ve started drinking tea. · 이어서 How did you do it?
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) drinking coffee / drinking tea → I gave up drinking coffee. I’ve started drinking tea. · 이어서 How did you do it? The items (the words the learner gets for each one): drinking coffee / drinking tea | eating late / going to bed early | taking the bus / cycling to work | snacking / eating fruit.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "Old habits die hard." (습관 바꾸기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I’m trying to ___." / "I gave up ___ing." / "I’ve started ___ing.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I’ve started going to bed earlier.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 바꾸는 습관 말하기: "I’m trying to eat healthier." (더 건강하게 먹으려고 노력 중이에요., 보통); "I quit drinking coffee." (커피를 끊었어요., 보통); "I’ve started going to bed earlier." (더 일찍 자기 시작했어요., 보통)
- 어려움과 나아진 점 말하기: "It’s harder than I thought." (생각보다 어려워요., 보통); "Old habits die hard." (오랜 습관은 잘 안 고쳐져요., 친근); "I keep forgetting." (자꾸 잊어버려요., 보통); "I’m doing better now." (이제 좀 나아졌어요., 보통)
- 묻고 답하기: "How did you do it?" (어떻게 했어요?, 보통); "Little by little." (조금씩요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: give up · quit · stop

He *gave up* smoking. 담배를 끊었어요.
She *quit* drinking alcohol. 술을 끊었어요.
I *stopped* eating late. 밤늦게 먹는 걸 그만뒀어요.
‘그만두다’ 뜻일 때 셋 다 뒤에 -ing. give up은 ‘애써 끊다’ 느낌이에요.
운동할 때 쓰는 말

*bend* your knees 무릎을 굽히다 · *stretch* your *muscles* 근육을 늘이다
lift *weights* 역기를 들다 · swim at the *pool* 수영장에서 수영하다
*football* 축구(미국에서는 soccer, football은 미식축구)
My alarm *goes off* at six. 알람이 6시에 울려요.
steps.blank:
A: I’m trying ___ eat healthier.   B: Good for you! How did you ___ it?
A: I gave up ___ sugar in my coffee. It’s harder ___ I thought.   B: Little by ___!
낱말 상자: to · do · putting · than · little
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- give up · quit · stop: He gave up smoking. 담배를 끊었어요. / She quit drinking alcohol. 술을 끊었어요. / I stopped eating late. 밤늦게 먹는 걸 그만뒀어요. / ‘그만두다’ 뜻일 때 셋 다 뒤에 -ing. give up은 ‘애써 끊다’ 느낌이에요.
- 운동할 때 쓰는 말: bend your knees 무릎을 굽히다 · stretch your muscles 근육을 늘이다 / lift weights 역기를 들다 · swim at the pool 수영장에서 수영하다 / football 축구(미국에서는 soccer, football은 미식축구) / My alarm goes off at six. 알람이 6시에 울려요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: I’m trying ___ eat healthier. B: Good for you! How did you ___ it? / A: I gave up ___ sugar in my coffee. It’s harder ___ I thought. B: Little by ___! / 낱말 상자: to · do · putting · than · little
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: stretch (스트레칭하다, 늘이다), screen (화면), cycle (자전거를 타다), pool (수영장), ball (공), football (축구; 축구공), coach (코치, 감독), weight (무게; (운동용) 역기·아령), smoke (연기; 담배를 피우다), healthy (건강한, 건강에 좋은), sugar (설탕). Review words: exercise (운동; 운동하다).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: I gave up eating late at night.
I try to avoid sugar at night.
food with less fat and sugar
I want to stay active in winter.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: give (주다(give up ~ing ~을 그만두다)) — "I gave up eating late at night."; habit (습관) — "Old habits die hard."; quit (그만두다, 끊다) — "I quit drinking coffee."; routine ((매일 하는) 일과) — "my morning routine"; healthier (더 건강한(healthy의 비교급)) — "I’m trying to eat healthier."; effort (노력) — "Changing a habit takes effort."; avoid (피하다) — "I try to avoid sugar at night."; fat (지방) — "food with less fat and sugar"; physical (몸의, 신체의) — "Walking is good physical activity."; active (활동적인) — "I want to stay active in winter.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Is there a habit you’re trying to change?
Have you ever given up something?
Yes, I gave up ___ing. / Not yet.
What have you started doing lately?
What’s hard about changing a habit?
It’s harder than I thought. / I keep forgetting.
How do you stay active in winter?
I walk a lot. / I’ve started ___ing.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Is there a habit you’re trying to change?" (hint on screen: Yes. I’m trying to ___.)
- "Have you ever given up something?" (hint on screen: Yes, I gave up ___ing. / Not yet.)
- "What have you started doing lately?" (hint on screen: I’ve started ___ing.)
- "What’s hard about changing a habit?" (hint on screen: It’s harder than I thought. / I keep forgetting.)
- "How do you stay active in winter?" (hint on screen: I walk a lot. / I’ve started ___ing.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Ben’s Sunday Team
steps.text: This year, Ben has started cycling to work, and on Sundays he plays football with a local team. His teammates from other countries call it football, but Ben still says “soccer”! Their coach is sixty and very active. Before every game, he says, “Bend your knees and stretch your muscles first.” He used to smoke, but he gave up cigarettes twenty years ago. He also asks the team to avoid alcohol the night before a game. Last Sunday, Ben’s bike broke on the way, and the coach helped him *sort out* the problem. Now Ben’s alarm *goes off* an hour early on Sundays.
steps.gloss: teammate 팀 동료 · bend 굽히다 · knee 무릎 · muscle 근육 · cigarette 담배 · alcohol 술 · sort out (문제를) 해결하다, 바로잡다 · go off (알람이) 울리다
questions: What does the coach say before every game?
What happened to Ben’s bike last Sunday?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Ben’s Sunday Team". Text: "This year, Ben has started cycling to work, and on Sundays he plays football with a local team. His teammates from other countries call it football, but Ben still says “soccer”! Their coach is sixty and very active. Before every game, he says, “Bend your knees and stretch your muscles first.” He used to smoke, but he gave up cigarettes twenty years ago. He also asks the team to avoid alcohol the night before a game. Last Sunday, Ben’s bike broke on the way, and the coach helped him sort out the problem. Now Ben’s alarm goes off an hour early on Sundays." Words: teammate 팀 동료 · bend 굽히다 · knee 무릎 · muscle 근육 · cigarette 담배 · alcohol 술 · sort out (문제를) 해결하다, 바로잡다 · go off (알람이) 울리다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What does the coach say before every game?" / "What happened to Ben’s bike last Sunday?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘I’m trying to ___.’로 요즘 바꾸려고 애쓰는 습관을 말할 수 있어요.
‘I gave up ___ing.’로 그만둔 습관을 말할 수 있어요.
‘I’ve started ___ing.’로 새로 시작한 습관을 말하고 ‘How did you do it?’으로 물을 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘I’m trying to ___.’로 요즘 바꾸려고 애쓰는 습관을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘I gave up ___ing.’로 그만둔 습관을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘I’ve started ___ing.’로 새로 시작한 습관을 말하고 ‘How did you do it?’으로 물을 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 내 고향
steps.goal: 자란 곳을 소개하고 지금도 가는지 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 12월 말 저녁, 회사 근처 작은 식당에서 열린 연말 모임. 창가 테이블에서 마야가 휴대폰 속 바닷가 항구 마을 사진을 보여 주고, 지우가 따뜻한 차를 들고 웃으며 들여다봄. 뒤쪽 테이블에서 클로이와 동료들이 웃고 있음(간판·화면에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Where did you grow up?" (내 고향). Goal: 자란 곳을 소개하고 지금도 가는지 말하기. Today's scene: 12월 말 저녁, 회사 근처 작은 식당에서 열린 연말 모임. 창가 테이블에서 마야가 휴대폰 속 바닷가 항구 마을 사진을 보여 주고, 지우가 따뜻한 차를 들고 웃으며 들여다봄. 뒤쪽 테이블에서 클로이와 동료들이 웃고 있음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Maya, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I grew up in ___.".

steps.when: 어린 시절을 보낸 곳을 말해요. grow up의 과거형은 *grew up*, 곳 앞에는 in.
steps.extra: I grew up in Seoul. · I grew up in a small village.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I grew up in ___." (~에서 자랐어요.). When to use it: 어린 시절을 보낸 곳을 말해요. grow up의 과거형은 grew up, 곳 앞에는 in. Note: I grew up in Seoul. · I grew up in a small village.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "It’s a small town near ___.".

steps.when: 상대가 모르는 곳을 설명할 때, 근처의 잘 알려진 곳을 함께 말해요.
steps.extra: It’s a small town near the sea. · It’s a small town near a big port.
steps.teach:

Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:

(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I go back there ___.".

steps.when: 지금도 고향에 가는지, 얼마나 자주 가는지 말해요. there 앞에는 to 없이.
steps.extra: I go back there once a year. · I go back there every summer.

steps.title: Back Home · 12월 말 저녁, 연말 모임에서

lines.en: Jiwoo, any plans for the holidays?
lines.ko: 지우 씨, 연휴에 계획 있어요?

lines.en: I’m visiting my grandma’s village. What about you, Maya?
lines.ko: 할머니 마을에 가요. 마야는요?

lines.en: I’m going home! {{I grew up in}} a suburb of Atlanta. Now my parents live by the sea. {{It’s a small town near}} a big port.
lines.ko: 저는 집에 가요! 애틀랜타 근교에서 자랐어요. 지금은 부모님이 바닷가에 사세요. 큰 항구 도시 근처의 작은 마을이에요.

lines.en: Sounds lovely! Do you go back there often?
lines.ko: 좋네요! 거기 자주 가요?

lines.en: {{I go back there}} once a year, for the holidays. It’s a quiet place, and everybody knows everybody!
lines.ko: 일 년에 한 번, 연휴에 가요. 조용한 곳이라 다들 서로 알아요!

lines.en: Ha! And Atlanta? Do you still visit?
lines.ko: 하하! 애틀랜타는요? 지금도 가요?

lines.en: Sometimes. It’s changed a lot. But in my parents’ town, not much happens. In a way, that’s what I love. Where did you grow up?
lines.ko: 가끔요. 많이 변했어요. 그런데 부모님 마을은 별일이 없어요. 어떻게 보면 그게 좋아요. 지우 씨는 어디서 자랐어요?

lines.en: In Seoul. But my grandma’s village feels like my hometown. It’s surrounded by mountains.
lines.ko: 서울이요. 그런데 할머니 마을이 고향처럼 느껴져요. 산으로 둘러싸여 있어요.

lines.en: It must be so quiet out there. Oh, and Jiwoo… my team is hiring in the new year. Would you like to apply?
lines.ko: 거긴 정말 조용하겠네요. 아, 그리고 지우 씨… 우리 팀이 새해에 사람을 뽑아요. 지원해 볼래요?

lines.en: Really? Wow… I’ll think about it.
lines.ko: 정말요? 와… 생각해 볼게요.

8. Jiwoo: "In Seoul. But my grandma’s village feels like my hometown. It’s surrounded by mountains." (서울이요. 그런데 할머니 마을이 고향처럼 느껴져요. 산으로 둘러싸여 있어요.)
9. Maya: "It must be so quiet out there. Oh, and Jiwoo… my team is hiring in the new year. Would you like to apply?" (거긴 정말 조용하겠네요. 아, 그리고 지우 씨… 우리 팀이 새해에 사람을 뽑아요. 지원해 볼래요?)
10. Jiwoo: "Really? Wow… I’ll think about it." (정말요? 와… 생각해 볼게요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too; never correct that. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Maya. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

frame: Where did you grow up? / Do you go back there often?
I grew up in ___. It’s a small town near ___. / I go back there ___.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: Where did you grow up? / Do you go back there often? / I grew up in ___. It’s a small town near ___. / I go back there ___. Table (자란 곳 → 어떤 곳):
- I grew up in a small town. → It’s by the sea.
- I grew up in the countryside. → It’s surrounded by mountains.
- I grew up in a big city. → It’s changed a lot.
- I grew up in a village. → Not much happens there.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I *grew up in* a small town. 작은 마을에서 자랐어요.
지나간 일이라 과거형 *grew*(grow–grew), 자란 곳 앞에는 *in*.
‘태어나다’는 was born: I was born in Seoul.

I *go back there* once a year. 일 년에 한 번 거기 가요.
I *go back for* the holidays. 연휴에 (고향에) 가요.
there 앞에는 to 없이: go back there · go back *to* my hometown
errors: I go back to there every year.
I go back there every year.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- grow up in + 곳: I grew up in a small town. 작은 마을에서 자랐어요. / 지나간 일이라 과거형 grew(grow–grew), 자란 곳 앞에는 in. / ‘태어나다’는 was born: I was born in Seoul.
- go back there + 언제: I go back there once a year. 일 년에 한 번 거기 가요. / I go back for the holidays. 연휴에 (고향에) 가요. / there 앞에는 to 없이: go back there · go back to my hometown
Common mistakes on screen:
- I grew up at Seoul. → I grew up in Seoul. (도시·마을 이름 앞에는 in.)
- I go back to there every year. → I go back there every year. (there 앞에는 to를 쓰지 않아요.)
- It’s surround by mountains. → It’s surrounded by mountains. (‘둘러싸여 있다’는 be surrounded by.)
- Everybody know everybody. → Everybody knows everybody. (everybody는 한 사람처럼 knows.)
There are 2 grammar points and 4 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: grow up in + 곳: I grew up in a small town. 작은 마을에서 자랐어요.지나간 일이라 과거형 grew(grow–grew), 자란 곳 앞에는 in.‘태어나다’는 was born: I was born in Seoul.
go back there + 언제: I go back there once a year. 일 년에 한 번 거기 가요.I go back for the holidays. 연휴에 (고향에) 가요.there 앞에는 to 없이: go back there · go back to my hometown
mistakes: I grew up at Seoul. → I grew up in Seoul.
I go back to there every year. → I go back there every year.
It’s surround by mountains. → It’s surrounded by mountains.
Everybody know everybody. → Everybody knows everybody.

steps.note: 예) a small town / once a year → I grew up in a small town. I go back there once a year. · 선생님이 What’s it like? 하고 이어 물어요.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) a small town / once a year → I grew up in a small town. I go back there once a year. · 선생님이 What’s it like? 하고 이어 물어요. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): a small town / once a year | the countryside / for the holidays | a port city / every summer | a village / twice a year.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "Where did you grow up?" (내 고향); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I grew up in ___." / "It’s a small town near ___." / "I go back there ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I go back for the holidays.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 고향 소개하기: "It’s by the sea." (바닷가에 있어요., 보통); "It’s surrounded by mountains." (산으로 둘러싸여 있어요., 보통); "It’s changed a lot." (많이 변했어요., 보통); "Not much happens there." (별일 없는 조용한 곳이에요., 친근); "Everybody knows everybody." (다들 서로 알아요., 친근)
- 지금도 가는지 말하기: "My parents still live there." (부모님이 아직 거기 사세요., 보통); "I go back for the holidays." (연휴에 (고향에) 가요., 보통)
- 초대하기: "You should come visit." (한번 놀러 와요., 친근); "I’ll show you around." (구경시켜 줄게요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: hometown (고향), countryside (시골), coast (해안, 바닷가), land (땅, 육지), horse (말), farmer (농부), band (악단, 밴드), fan (팬), gather (모이다), surround (둘러싸다), valley (골짜기, 계곡), harbor (항구).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.
